title: Project-suppression gate is structurally dead for local-only (remoteless) repos — every in-project continuation fires a false search_miss
location: _caller_in_top_hit_project, lines 536-547 (caller_origin.repo is None -> return False; mem.origin.repo is None -> continue)
description: The gate that suppresses the dominant false-miss cohort (the module's own comment: 'Dogfood evidence (2.7.x): ~95% of replayable misses came from this cohort' — in-project continuations like 'update X', 'push it') keys exclusively on git REMOTE identity: it returns False when caller_origin.repo is None (line 536) and skips any memory whose origin.repo is None (line 543), with no worktree_root or cwd fallback. A repo created with git init and never given a remote (scratch projects, private notes repos, pre-first-push projects) gets repo=None from origin.capture() — and capture() additionally nulls worktree_root when there is no remote (origin.py:117-118, 'worktree_root = _git_worktree_root(resolved) if repo_url else None'), so even the data a fallback would need is discarded at write time. Result: for remoteless repos the entire ~95% cohort of false misses returns — identical user behavior produces verdict 'ok' when the repo has a remote and 'miss' when it does not, polluting search_miss telemetry and memory_health silent-miss rates.
example_input: Memory 'zephyrnotes release process: run scripts/release.sh from the repo root, then tag.' scoped projects:zephyrnotes, written from a git-init-only repo (origin.repo=None); user message 'run the zephyrnotes release' from inside that repo, no retrieval events
expected: verdict 'ok' — caller is inside the same project the memory was written from (the gate suppresses exactly this when a remote exists)
actual: verdict 'miss' (search_miss emitted); the same scenario with repo='git@github.com:mattias/zephyrnotes.git' on both sides yields 'ok'
verifier_notes: CONFIRMED. The repro runs as claimed at HEAD 874b0b0: identical memory body, scope (projects:zephyrnotes), query, and caller cwd yield verdict 'ok' when origin.repo is a remote URL on both sides and 'miss' when the repo is git-init-only (repo=None). All cited code locations check out: audit.py:536 returns False whenever caller_origin.repo is None, audit.py:543 skips any memory with origin.repo None, and origin.py:118 ('worktree_root = _git_worktree_root(resolved) if repo_url else None') discards worktree_root at write time for remoteless repos — the capture() docstring frames that gating purely as a subprocess-saving shortcut, not a semantic decision, so the data a fallback would need is lost incidentally. Reachable in production: both the Stop hook (hook.py:236) and the MCP audit_turn handler (handlers/audit_turn.py:125) capture origin live from the turn's cwd, which yields repo=None in a remoteless checkout. NOT a documented trade-off: the gate's docstring (audit.py:512-535) explains its two predicates but never addresses remoteless repos; the introducing commit eabe63c is silent on it; the four gate tests in tests/test_audit.py (cross-repo, URL normalization, legacy origin=None, non-projects scope) pin neighboring behavior but nothing pins remoteless→miss as intended; CHANGELOG has no mention. The None-checks themselves are deliberate conservatism (repos_match(None,None) returns True — wildcard semantics that would over-suppress for callers outside any repo), but that expl
suggested_fix: Two-part minimal fix preserving the gate's conservative require-positive-evidence design. (1) origin.py capture(): probe _git_worktree_root(resolved) FIRST and gate the remote/branch lookups on its result instead of gating worktree_root on repo_url — subprocess count stays flat (non-repo cwd: 1 call as today; repo with remote: 3 calls as today; remoteless repo: 2-3 calls), and remoteless writes retain worktree_root (and branch). (2) audit.py _caller_in_top_hit_project: keep the 'caller_origin is None -> False' early return, but let a caller with repo=None and worktree_root set fall through to the loop; inside the loop, suppress when EITHER (both repos non-None and repos_match) OR (mem.origin.worktree_root is not None and caller_origin.worktree_root is not None and they compare equal as resolved paths). Do NOT reuse worktrees_match() here — its either-side-null->True wildcard semantics would over-suppress; strict both-set equality is the positive evidence the gate's docstring demands. Legacy remoteless memories written before the capture() fix still carry worktree_root=None and remain unsuppressed, consistent with the existing legacy origin=None treatment. Add tests pinning: remoteless same-worktree -> ok, remoteless different-worktree -> miss, remoteless caller vs legacy (worktree_root=None) memory -> miss, and a capture() test that a git-init-no-remote tmpdir yields worktree_root set with repo=None.

title: Two-word acknowledgments built from non-stopword filler ('all done', 'looks good', 'sounds good') clear the MIN_PROBE_CONTENT_TOKENS gate and score 2/2 = 'high' against ordinary memory bodies — false search_miss on bare continuations
location: probe_for_miss, single-content-token gate at line 401 + v1 threshold at lines 461-466 (with the conservative _STOPWORDS list in search.py:78-141)
description: The gate's stated purpose is to drop bare continuations as no_signal ('bare continuations like yes / continue / go for it structurally carry no signal', lines 58-64), implemented as 'fewer than 2 content tokens after stopword strip'. But the most common end-of-turn acknowledgments are two DISTINCT words that are not in the deliberately short stopword list: 'all done', 'looks good', 'sounds good', 'option 2' (answering an assistant's clarifying question). These legitimately count 2 content tokens, pass the gate, and the v1 rule then needs only both words to co-occur anywhere in one memory body for coverage 2/2 = 'high'. Ordinary bodies satisfy this constantly ('Once the migration is done, delete all the temp tables' matches 'all done'; 'Looks like ruff and mypy must both pass; ... good enough only on docs-only diffs' matches 'looks good'). Each such turn emits a search_miss against a top hit that has nothing to do with the user's (content-free) message. Distinct from the already-reported duplicate-token ('yes yes') and contraction-fragment ('what's' -> s) gate bypasses: here both tokens are real, distinct words — the failure is the stopword list's lack of conversational filler combined with the 2-token coverage rule, not token-counting artifacts.
example_input: user message 'all done' (or 'looks good', 'sounds good') against a store containing 'Once the migration is done, delete all the temp tables in staging.'
expected: verdict 'no_signal' (or at least 'ok') — a bare acknowledgment carries no retrieval intent; this is exactly the noise class the gate documents itself as dropping
actual: verdict 'miss' with top-1 relevance 'high'; search_miss emitted against an irrelevant memory for all three acknowledgments
verifier_notes: CONFIRMED, attempted refutation failed on every front. (1) Repro is exact: all three acknowledgments score 2/2 coverage = 'high' (search.py:189, coverage >= 0.75) and return verdict 'miss' under the default hybrid mode — the same mode the production Stop hook passes (hook.py:265, cfg.behavior.search_mode or 'hybrid'). (2) Not a documented trade-off: the module docstring (audit.py:58-64) and the gate comment (audit.py:115-124) state the gate's purpose is dropping 'bare continuations' as no_signal, and the gate commit (0a1daa1 'fix(audit): drop bare-continuation false positives via content-token gate') was created precisely to kill this noise class — the cited dogfood evidence says the single-token cohort alone was ~26% of search_miss events. 'all done'/'looks good'/'sounds good' are unambiguously bare continuations that bypass the gate because 'all', 'done', 'looks', 'sounds', 'good' are absent from the deliberately-short _STOPWORDS list (search.py:78-141). The only test pinning the 2-token floor (tests/test_audit.py:178, test_two_content_token_query_passes_the_gate) guards against suppressing legitimate queries like 'backup strategy'; no test or doc accepts the filler class. (3) Production mitigations do NOT shield this: (a) the retrieval shield requires a search/show/list event in the 60s lookback, but bare-ack turns are exactly the turns where the opt-in discipline correctly produces no search; (b) _caller_in_top_hit_project (audit.py:507-547) only suppresses hits with a pr
suggested_fix: Widen the gate's definition of 'bare continuation' inside audit.py only — do NOT touch search.py's _STOPWORDS (the comment at search.py:72-77 is right that 'good'/'done'/'all' must stay searchable as body/query terms). Add a module-level frozenset next to MIN_PROBE_CONTENT_TOKENS, e.g. _ACK_TOKENS = frozenset({'ok','okay','yes','yep','yeah','sure','thanks','thank','please','good','great','nice','perfect','cool','fine','done','all','looks','sounds','lgtm','go','ahead','ship','proceed','continue','works','agreed','correct','right','exactly'}), and extend the gate at audit.py:401: after computing content = _strip_stopwords(tokenize(user_message)), return no_signal when len(content) < MIN_PROBE_CONTENT_TOKENS OR all(t in _ACK_TOKENS for t in content). A mixed message ('looks good, now update the backup docs') still passes because 'update'/'backup'/'docs' are not in the set, so the existing test_two_content_token_query_passes_the_gate pin ('backup strategy' -> miss) is preserved, and the v1 threshold rule is untouched. Document the new set in the module docstring's gate paragraph (audit.py:58-64) as the all-filler cohort, add a test mirroring test_single_content_token_query_returns_no_signal for ('all done','looks good','sounds good','sounds great','ship it now'<-this one should still pass the gate? no: 'ship','it'(stopword)... choose non-ambiguous cases), and note in CHANGELOG that historical events can be invalidated with the existing 'bettermemory consolidate --acknowledge-misses-before <ts>' cutoff — the same mechanism used for the v2.7.3 cwd-suppression change (docs/eval.md:53).

title: v1 threshold reads only the rank-1 hit: a 3/3 'high'-relevance answer at rank 2 is swallowed when a fresher, term-frequency-heavy partial match wins the score ranking
location: probe_for_miss, lines 461-466 (top_hit = top_hits[0]; clears_threshold = top_hit.relevance == 'high')
description: Score order and the coverage-based relevance label are computed from different signals (search.py: score = tf + 2x scope-token bonus + recency multiplier vs. relevance = matched_unique/query_unique), so they routinely invert: a recent, verbose note that repeats one query term many times (plus a scope-token hit, e.g. scope 'tools:grafana') outranks an older memory that precisely matches ALL query terms. The probe retains 3 hits explicitly 'so a curation pass can replay the decision' (_TOP_HITS_RETAINED) but the verdict only inspects hits[0].relevance — a 'high' hit at rank 2 or 3 with zero retrieval events in the window yields verdict 'ok' and the silent miss is never flagged. In the repro the store is ordinary: one fresh chatty ops note mentioning 'grafana' five times, one older precise fact ('Grafana dashboard config lives at /data/compose/grafana/provisioning...'), and routine filler memories that make 'dashboard'/'config' common corpus terms. Hybrid fusion puts the chatty note first (relevance 'low', matched only 'grafana'); the exact answer sits at rank 2 with relevance 'high'; verdict comes back 'ok'. This is the exact fresh-verbose-note-vs-old-precise-fact shape real stores accumulate, and it defeats the audit on precisely the turns it exists for.
example_input: user message 'where is the grafana dashboard config?' against a store with a fresh multi-sentence grafana-access note (scope tools:grafana) and an older 'Grafana dashboard config lives at /data/compose/grafana/provisioning/dashboards' memory, plus ordinary filler; no retrieval events
expected: verdict 'miss' — a high-relevance hit for the turn's query exists in the probe's own retained top hits and no retrieval happened
actual: verdict 'ok'; top-1 relevance 'low' (matched ['grafana'] only), rank-2 relevance 'high' (matched ['config','dashboard','grafana']) is never consulted
verifier_notes: Repro confirmed verbatim at HEAD 874b0b0. Diagnostics: rank-1 = fresh chatty note, score 0.0328, relevance 'low' (matched only 'grafana'); rank-2 = precise old fact, score 0.0323, relevance 'high' (full coverage); verdict 'ok'. Same inversion under mode='keyword', so it is not hybrid-fusion-specific. Mechanism verified in search.py: score blends TF/BM25 + 2x scope-token bonus + recency multiplier (search.py:203-209, 346-362), while the relevance label is pure coverage matched_unique/query_unique (search.py:179-193) — they are independent signals and invert on near-ties. Refutation attempts failed: (a) the v1 rule is documented as top-1, but the module's own contract language says 'a high-relevance hit exists' (audit.py:12-14 and MissReport docstring audit.py:177-179) — the implementation (audit.py:465-466) is narrower than its documented semantics; (b) the inline trade-off comment (audit.py:461-464) only weighs label-strictness alternatives (all-3-high vs medium) and never considers the rank-inversion case; (c) the suppression gate _caller_in_top_hit_project scans ALL retained top hits (audit.py:539) while the trigger checks only hits[0] — an asymmetry indicating oversight, not design; (d) the calibration machinery the docstring points to cannot discover this class: eval.py:816-825 explicitly states the threshold sweep replays only search_miss events and turn_audited carries no top_hits, so v1 false negatives leave zero replayable trace and v1_drift can never surface them. No
suggested_fix: Minimal, conservatism-preserving fix in /Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/audit.py: change the threshold check from `top_hits[0].relevance == "high"` to `any(h.relevance == "high" for h in top_hits)` — it only consults the 3 hits already retained (_TOP_HITS_RETAINED), still requires >= 0.75 content-token coverage, and leaves every other gate (MIN_PROBE_CONTENT_TOKENS, recent-retrieval shield, _caller_in_top_hit_project suppression — which already scans all top hits) unchanged, so the documented conservative design holds. Three companion changes keep the versioned-rule contract honest: (1) bump the rule id — add e.g. THRESHOLD_RULE_V1_1 = "v1.1_any_top3_high" and record it on reports/events instead of silently changing v1's meaning; (2) register the matching pure rule in eval.THRESHOLD_RULES so future sweeps can replay it; (3) in eval.compute_threshold_sweep, key the reference rule / v1_drift validation on the threshold_rule recorded on each event (or on the new rule) rather than hard-pinning v1_top1_high, otherwise post-fix logs would report spurious v1_drift. Optionally (larger change, addresses the structural blind spot): carry top_hits on turn_audited events so future looser-rule calibration has a replayable corpus — eval.py:816-825 documents that limitation today.

title: Lookback window has no anchor at turn start: an unrelated search from the PREVIOUS turn within 60s shields a fresh miss in the next turn
location: _count_recent_retrievals, lines 571-584 (single cutoff = now - lookback_seconds; any in-window retrieval event counts), consumed at probe_for_miss lines 468-482
description: The module docstring claims the 60s window is 'short enough that a search from two turns ago doesn't paper over a fresh miss' (lines 66-70) — but that only holds for slow turns. In a normal rapid exchange (model searches at T+0s for topic X, replies at T+5s; user sends a new message about topic Y at T+20s; model answers Y from priors without searching; Stop hook audits at T+35s), the previous turn's X search at T+0s is inside the [now-60s, now] window, recent_retrieval_count comes back 1, and the fresh Y miss is verdict 'ok'. Quick consecutive turns are the dominant interaction pattern in chat sessions, so this systematically under-counts misses exactly when sessions are most active. Distinct from the already-reported long-turn finding (search earlier than 60s in the SAME turn producing a false 'miss' — false-positive direction): this is the opposite direction and the opposite boundary — the window extends backward across the turn boundary with no lower anchor at the current turn's start, because the wall-clock heuristic has no notion of when the audited turn began.
example_input: events: one 'search' event (query 'pytest fixtures', same session) 35s before the audit; current user message 'where is the grafana dashboard config?' with a high-relevance grafana memory in the store and no search this turn
expected: verdict 'miss' — no retrieval happened for THIS turn; the 35s-old search belonged to the previous, unrelated turn
actual: verdict 'ok' with recent_retrieval_count=1 — the previous turn's unrelated search papers over the fresh miss
verifier_notes: Confirmed despite the default-refute stance. The repro reproduces verbatim at HEAD 874b0b0: an unrelated 'pytest fixtures' search event 35s old in the same session shields a fresh high-relevance grafana miss (verdict 'ok', recent_retrieval_count=1, top1 'high'). Code matches the claim: _count_recent_retrievals (/Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/audit.py:571-584) uses a single cutoff = now - lookback_seconds with no lower anchor at the audited turn's start, and is topic-agnostic (never reads the event's query/returned); probe_for_miss:481-482 shields on count>0. The production Stop hook hard-codes lookback_seconds=60 (/Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/hook.py:260), so the cross-turn-boundary case is the live path. NOT a documented trade-off: the module docstring (audit.py:66-70) asserts the 60s window is 'short enough that a search from two turns ago doesn't paper over a fresh miss' — demonstrably false whenever consecutive turns complete within 60s, a common cadence in active sessions. No test pins this: every shielding test in tests/test_audit.py uses a topically related search (returned=[m.id]); none covers an unrelated previous-turn retrieval inside the window. Input shape is realistic (homelab grafana memory, natural query, event dict matches recorder schema). Severity medium, not high: (1) when the prior-turn retrieval was same-topic, shielding is arguably correct — the retrieved content is still in the model's
suggested_fix: Add an optional turn-start anchor while preserving the conservative (anti-false-positive) design: (1) Add `turn_started_at: datetime | None = None` to probe_for_miss and _count_recent_retrievals in /Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/audit.py; when provided, clamp the window lower bound to `cutoff = max(now - timedelta(seconds=lookback_seconds), ensure_utc(turn_started_at))`. (2) In hook.py's _extract_last_exchange, also capture the latest user row's `timestamp` field from the Claude Code transcript JSONL (the hook already walks these rows) and thread it through run_audit -> probe_for_miss; fall back to None (exact current behavior) when the field is absent/unparseable, so the change degrades gracefully and in-process MCP callers are unaffected until they opt in. (3) To avoid converting legitimate same-topic follow-ups (model answering from content retrieved last turn) into new false 'miss' flags — the direction the project's design treats as worse — keep counting pre-anchor events inside the full lookback window when they plausibly covered the probed topic: a `search` event whose `returned` ids intersect the probe's top-hit ids, or a `show`/`list` event whose memory_id/ids intersect them. (4) Update the module docstring design note (audit.py:66-70) to describe the anchor + relatedness carve-out instead of the now-disproven 'short enough' claim, and add two tests: unrelated previous-turn search inside the window with an anchor -> 'miss'; related (id-overlapping) previous-turn search inside the window with an anchor -> 'ok'.

title: Symmetric kebab expansion multiplies shared compound identifiers, pushing distinct per-environment facts over the Jaccard dedup threshold
location: _find_dedup_jaccard (consolidate.py:297-329, token sets built at line 301 via _content_token_set, search.py:1005-1015 / _expand_kebab search.py:153-172)
description: The dedup token set runs _expand_kebab symmetrically, so a shared compound identifier like 'docker-compose' contributes THREE intersection tokens (docker-compose, docker, compose) while the one meaning-bearing token that differs ('prod' vs 'dev') contributes only one union element each side. For the canonical memory shape 'Use <shared-tool-file> for <shared-thing>' where two genuinely distinct facts differ only in an environment/file qualifier, raw stopword-stripped Jaccard is 0.714 (below the 0.75 threshold) but the kebab-expanded similarity the pass actually uses is 0.778 — the expansion alone flips the pair over the line. find_dedup_candidates then proposes (and `consolidate --apply` commits) tombstoning the older memory, destroying a real fact about the prod compose file because a dev-counterpart fact exists. Any pair of memories citing the same hyphenated tool/identifier (docker-compose, pre-commit, sentence-transformers, uptime-kuma) plus 3-4 shared plain words is exposed.
example_input: Memory A: 'Use docker-compose.prod.yml for the homelab stack' (updated 20d ago); Memory B: 'Use docker-compose.dev.yml for the homelab stack' (updated today)
expected: Two distinct facts (prod vs dev compose file) — no dedup candidate; raw token overlap is 0.714, under the 0.75 threshold
actual: Flagged as near-duplicates at similarity 0.778 (kebab expansion adds 'docker'+'compose' to the intersection); on --apply the prod-file memory is tombstoned and only the dev-file memory survives
verifier_notes:
CONFIRMED despite adversarial stance. Repro output verbatim: raw jaccard 0.714, expanded jaccard 0.778, method jaccard, "FLAGGED sim=0.778: keep 'Use docker-compose.dev.yml for the homelab stack' / tombstone 'Use docker-compose.prod.yml for the homelab stack'". The kebab expansion alone flips the pair over the 0.75 threshold exactly as claimed.

Refutation attempts and why they failed:
1. "Documented trade-off?" The symmetric expansion IS documented as deliberate in _content_token_set (/Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/search.py:1005-1015), but the docstring's safety argument — "Inflating set size on the kebab side is the cost — accepted because the union grows in proportion and Jaccard stays well-behaved" — is mathematically false for the shared-compound case. Adding k expansion tokens to BOTH sides adds k to intersection and k to union, and (i+k)/(u+k) > i/u strictly whenever i<u, so a shared compound can only inflate similarity. The documented rationale covers the one-sided case (kebab vs spaced-out notation, where expansion grows union only and deflates similarity); the inflation case is an unexamined side effect, not an accepted cost. The only test pinning symmetric expansion (test_find_similar_kebab_expansion_is_symmetric, /Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/tests/test_search.py:435-444) covers exactly the one-sided cross-notation case — nothing contemplates shared compounds.
2. "Contrived input?" No — short imperative fact memor
suggested_fix:
Make kebab expansion pairwise-aware instead of unconditionally symmetric: expand a compound token only when the joined form is ABSENT from the other side's raw token set. When both sides already contain the joined token (e.g. both say 'docker-compose'), agreement is fully counted by the token itself and the expansion sub-tokens add only inflation; when only one side has the compound, expansion still collapses cross-notation pairs (the documented purpose).

Concretely: add a small pairwise helper in search.py, e.g. _pair_similarity(raw_a, raw_b) where raw_x = set(_strip_stopwords(tokenize(text))) and each side's effective set is raw_x plus the kebab sub-tokens of only those compounds in raw_x that are not in the other side's raw set; compute Jaccard over those. Use it from both _find_dedup_jaccard (consolidate.py:301-315, precompute raw sets per memory instead of expanded sets) and the Jaccard branch of find_similar (search.py). Also correct the _content_token_set docstring's "union grows in proportion and Jaccard stays well-behaved" claim, which is false when the compound is shared.

Verified the fix preserves both behaviors: docker-compose prod/dev pair scores 0.714 (under threshold, not flagged); the existing cross-notation test case ('python-frontmatter ...' vs 'python frontmatter ...') scores 0.857 (still high), so test_find_similar_kebab_expansion_is_symmetric stays green. Add a regression test pinning the shared-compound pair below threshold (e.g. the docker-compose.prod.yml/dev.yml bodies from this repro) for both find_similar and find_dedup_candidates. This is minimal, deterministic, dependency-free, and preserves the module's conservative dedup design — it strictly removes false positives without weakening any documented true-positive case.

title: Keeper selection trusts `updated` as refinement authority, but metadata-only retags (including consolidate's own demotion) bump it — the ambient husk beats the verified fact and the fact is tombstoned
location: _pick_keeper Tier 1 (consolidate.py:247-248); demotion retag via store.update at consolidate.py:734-735; store.update stamps `updated` unconditionally (store.py:494-495) while memory_verify deliberately does NOT bump `updated` (store.py:470-473)
description: _pick_keeper's Tier-1 rule ('refining a memory implies that's the canonical version') keys on `updated`, but `updated` is bumped by every store.update — including the demotion pass's own category-only retag (consolidate.py:734-735) — while memory_verify attestation explicitly does NOT bump it. Realistic chain: a fact and its reworded duplicate sit at Jaccard 0.889 (between the 0.90 auto threshold and the 0.75 manual one), so the nightly auto-consolidate never dedups them but its demotion pass retags the retrieved-never-applied duplicate fact->ambient, stamping a fresh `updated`. The next manual `bettermemory consolidate --apply` finds the pair, crowns the just-retagged ambient husk keeper (newer `updated`), and tombstones the canonical fact along with its verified_paths attestation. Tier 2 ('attestation is authority') is unreachable because Tier 1 never ties. The dedup report's keep/drop signal points exactly backwards on legitimate input.
example_input: Fact (category=fact, verified_paths=['/opt/stacks/proxy/Caddyfile'], updated 60d ago, verified recently — verify doesn't bump updated) vs reworded duplicate retagged to ambient yesterday by the auto demotion pass (updated=1d ago)
expected: Keeper = the attested fact (canonical, verified); duplicate = the unattested ambient husk

title: Demotion's 'retrieved' criterion is relevance-blind: one rank-5 'low' ride-along hit makes an old fact demotion-eligible, even though the search event itself records the relevance the pass ignores
location: find_demotion_candidates (consolidate.py:398-417 retrieval counting; criteria at 427-437)
description: find_demotion_candidates counts a memory as 'retrieved' whenever its id appears anywhere in a search event's `returned` list, ignoring the parallel `relevance` list the search handler writes into the very same event (handlers/search.py:473-489). memory_search returns up to max_results=5 hits, so broad queries routinely pad ranks 3-5 with 'low'-relevance ride-alongs the model never reads (only the top hit is expanded). Those ride-alongs are also precisely the hits that escape the protective auto-applied event: the 2-turn use-token auto-commit (session.py DEFAULT_USE_TOKEN_TTL_TURNS=2) never fires when the search is the session's last memory_* call, and the Stop hook's substring attribution only rescues hits actually quoted in the reply. Net effect: a perfectly good 90-day-old fact that only ever appeared once as a low-relevance rank-5 hit in an end-of-session search satisfies created<cutoff, retrieved>0, applied==0 and is retagged fact->ambient — unattended, on the auto-consolidate Stop-hook path. The 'retrieved>0' gate that is supposed to separate dead weight ('the ranker surfaces it but the model gets no value') from cold memories is defeated by result-list padding.
example_input: fact 'Restic backup repo password lives in the macOS keychain entry homelab-restic' (created 90d ago, never applied) + one search event {kind: 'search', query: 'homelab', returned: [4 other ids, fact_id], relevance: ['high','high','medium','low','low']}

actual: DemotionCandidate produced (retrieved=1, fact -> ambient); committed unattended when the pass runs with apply=True
verifier_notes: Adversarial verification CONFIRMS the claim; could not refute it. (1) Repro reproduces verbatim on HEAD 874b0b0. (2) find_demotion_candidates (src/bettermemory/consolidate.py:411-417) counts any id in a search event's `returned` list while ignoring the parallel `relevance` list the search handler writes into the same event (src/bettermemory/handlers/search.py:478-479); health.py's dead_weight accumulator (health.py:985-989) is equally blind, so the docstring's 'mirrors dead_weight' framing is accurate but doesn't excuse it — health is report-only, the consolidate pass mutates. (3) The unattended path is real: hook.py:333-345 -> run_auto_consolidate -> consolidate(apply=True) commits fact->ambient with no review (gated on opt-in consolidate.auto_apply, default False — config.py:990). The model-callable memory_curate(dry_run=False) commits the same candidates. (4) The claimed protection gap is exact: all returned hits get use tokens, but auto-commit as `applied` requires a subsequent memory_* call >=2 turns later in the same server process (session.py:306-334, DEFAULT_USE_TOKEN_TTL_TURNS=2); the 30-min wall-clock eviction silently drops tokens WITHOUT committing (session.py:345-353); SessionState is in-memory; the Stop hook only attributes bodies substring-matched in the reply (hook.py:443+); only the top hit is expanded and only when relevance=='high' (handlers/search.py:400). suggested_fix: Minimal, conservative, preserves the documented mirror discipline: in find_demotion_candidates' search branch (consolidate.py:411-417), when the event carries a `relevance` list parallel to the canonical `returned` list (same length — it is written from the same `out` list at handlers/search.py:478-479), skip incrementing `retrieved` for ids whose label is 'low'. Legacy events (memory_ids/hit_ids fallbacks, or missing/length-mismatched relevance) keep the current count-everything behavior, so old logs are unaffected and the failure mode degrades to today's behavior, never worse. Memories whose only hits were 'low' then fall to retrieved==0 and land in the cold bucket, which is suggest-only — exactly the claim's expected disposition. Sketch: `rel = event.get('relevance'); ids = event.get('returned') or ...; for i, mid in enumerate(ids): if isinstance(rel, list) and len(rel) == len(ids) and rel[i] == 'low': continue; retrieved[mid] += 1` (apply the gate only on the canonical `returned` branch since legacy fields never carried relevance). title: Cold-scope pass with telemetry disabled: empty event log makes 'no applied events' vacuously true, flagging every stable scope older than 180 days for archiving
location: find_cold_scopes (consolidate.py:454-509); ungated CLI entry _cli_consolidate (cli/consolidate.py:229-290)
description: find_cold_scopes flags a scope when its newest memory is older than cold_scope_days AND no memory in the scope has an applied event. expected: No cold-scope suggestions — there is no usage evidence at all, so 'no applied events' is an absence-of-telemetry artifact, not a signal the scopes are dead

title: Retrieval questions ('Do you remember if/that ...?') are captured as fact proposals — explicit-marker override defeats the question reject, and 'remember i' prefix-matches 'remember if'
location: extract_proposals (lines 313-324) with _EXPLICIT_MARKERS (lines 70-86; 'remember that' line 71, 'remember i' line 73)
description: The explicit 'remember this' markers intentionally override the question/command reject so 'Can you remember that X?' is captured. But the markers are bare lowercase substrings, so they also fire on RETRIEVAL questions — the user asking the assistant what it already remembers, which is core usage of a memory product. 'Do you remember that we decided against Redis?' contains 'remember that'; worse, 'Do you remember if ...' fires because the marker 'remember i' is a string prefix of 'remember if' (substring match, no word boundary on the trailing token). Because is_explicit=True, both the endswith('?') reject and _QUESTION_OR_COMMAND_RE are skipped (lines 320-324), and the question is queued verbatim — trailing '?' and all — with suggested_category='fact', the highest-trust tier, which flows through accept by default (handlers/proposals.py line 91: 'category or match.suggested_category'). A question is never a stated fact: 'Do you remember if we already migrated the staging database to postgres 16?' may well be asked precisely because the migration did NOT happen.
example_input: Do you remember if we already migrated the staging database to postgres 16?
expected: Rejected — it is a question to the assistant (asks for retrieval, asserts nothing durable).

(3) NOT a documented trade-off: the comment at lines 67-69 justifies the override as 'when the user says any of these, they are asking to be remembered' — that premise is false for retrieval interrogatives ('Do you remember…?'), which ask what is ALREADY stored. The only tested override case is 'Can you remember that we deploy to fly.io…?' (tests/test_proposals.py:42-50), a capture request phrased politely; no test covers retrieval questions. The module docstring explicitly claims 'precision over recall by design' and warns that noisy proposals train the model to ignore the review surfac
suggested_fix: Two minimal changes in src/bettermemory/proposals.py, preserving the documented conservative design and the tested 'Can you remember that…?' override: (1) Fix the substring defect — match explicit markers with word boundaries instead of bare 'marker in low', e.g. compile _EXPLICIT_MARKERS into a single regex with \b on both ends (r"\b(?:remember that|remember to|remember i|remember we|note that|…)\b") so 'remember i' no longer prefix-matches 'remember if'/'remember it'. title: 'Make sure to/you ...' and 'Note that ...' — ubiquitous per-turn instructions and code commentary fire the explicit marker and are queued as durable 'fact' proposals
location: _EXPLICIT_MARKERS (lines 70-86; 'note that' line 75, 'make sure to' line 83, 'make sure you' line 84) used in extract_proposals line 314
description: The marker list comment claims 'High precision — when the user says any of these, they are asking to be remembered.' suggested_fix: Minimal and design-preserving: remove 'make sure to', 'make sure you', and 'note that' from _EXPLICIT_MARKERS in src/bettermemory/proposals.py (lines 75, 83, 84). The remaining markers ('remember that/to/i/we', 'keep in mind', 'for future reference', 'for the future', "don't forget", 'do not forget', 'from now on', 'going forward', 'always remember') all carry genuine remember-intent and uphold the 'high precision' comment. title: Length floor silently drops short explicit capture requests: 'Remember that I use zsh.' is never proposed
location: _MIN_CHARS/_MIN_TOKENS (lines 53-54) applied in _iter_candidate_sentences (lines 272-282) before any marker check in extract_proposals (line 312)
description: The 30-char / 6-token floor is applied to every sentence BEFORE the explicit-marker check, so the single highest-precision signal the module exists to capture — a literal 'remember that ...' request — is silently dropped whenever the remembered fact is short. The floor's rationale (lines 49-53) is filtering non-distinctive sentences like 'I like it.' for the bare-preference branch — but an explicit remember-request is self-evidently capture-worthy regardless of length (the marker itself eats ~14 of the 30 chars, so only facts longer than ~16 chars survive). expected: Proposed — an explicit 'remember that' capture request stating a durable tool preference.

verifier_notes: Repro confirmed at HEAD 874b0b0: both 'Remember that I use zsh.' (24 chars/5 tokens) and 'Remember that we use pnpm.' (26 chars/5 tokens) return []. title: NFD combining marks break tokenization: 'Tjörn' becomes ['tjo','rn'] — NFC queries miss NFD bodies entirely, and the dedup gate misses exact-text duplicates
location: _TOKEN_RE (line 66) / tokenize (line 144); also _content_token_set (line 1005) on the find_similar dedup path
description: Python re's \w does NOT match combining marks (category Mn, verified: re.match(r'\w', '̈') is None), so NFD-normalized text — the form macOS produces for filenames dragged from Finder, and common in text copied from PDFs/macOS apps — tokenizes catastrophically: NFD 'Tjörn' -> ['tjo','rn'], 'hänger' -> ['ha','nger'], 'på' -> ['pa'] (the base letter survives, the mark is dropped, and the word is SPLIT at the mark). A query typed normally (NFC 'tjörn') therefore never matches an NFD body in any Python ranker: a single-word query for the place name returns zero hits. The dedup gate is hit too: find_similar() on the byte-identical-looking NFC re-statement of an NFD memory scores 0.31 Jaccard (< 0.40 medium threshold) — an exact duplicate fact passes memory_write's dedup gate with no warning. This is a different mechanism from the already-reported FTS5-vs-Python diacritic-folding mismatch: it corrupts tokenization itself, fires with no index at all (stores under the 500-memory FTS threshold), and directly contradicts the comment at lines 55-61 claiming \w makes 'Niño café Mañana' tokenize correctly (true only in NFC). Fix shape: unicodedata.normalize('NFC', text) (or NFKC) before tokenizing.
example_input: memory body saved as NFD (pasted from macOS): 'Sommarstugan ligger på Tjörn; nyckeln hänger hos grannen Görel.'; query typed as NFC: 'Tjörn'
expected: the query matches the body's 'Tjörn'; find_similar flags the NFC re-write of the same sentence as a high-similarity duplicate
actual: search([m],'Tjörn') returns []; tokenize(nfd_body) yields ['sommarstugan','ligger','pa','tjo','rn','nyckeln','ha','nger','hos','grannen','go','rel']; find_similar(NFC duplicate, [NFD original]) returns []
verifier_notes: CONFIRMED, all three sub-claims. (1) Mechanism verified independently of the repro: re.match(r'\w', U+0308) is None — Python's \w excludes combining marks (category Mn) — so NFD 'Tjörn' (T j o U+0308 r n) tokenizes to ['tjo','rn']: the word is SPLIT at the mark, not merely accent-stripped. (2) The repro reproduces exactly: NFD body tokens = ['sommarstugan','ligger','pa','tjo','rn','nyckeln','ha','nger','hos','grannen','go','rel']; search([m],'Tjörn',mode='keyword') returns []; find_similar(NFC duplicate, [NFD original]) returns [] — an exact-text duplicate passes memory_write's dedup gate silently. (3) NOT a deliberate trade-off — the opposite: the same repo already fixed this exact failure class in /Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/attribution.py (_normalize, lines 237-252) with a docstring explaining that without NFC-first, non-ASCII text 'silently fails every tier', and tests/test_attribution.py deliberately constructs decomposed forms to pin it. search.py's tokenize (line 144) and the dedup _content_token_set (line 1015) never got the same treatment, and the comment at search.py:55-61 claiming \w makes 'Niño café Mañana' tokenize correctly holds only for NFC input — the regression test at tests/test_search.py:35-46 uses NFC literals only, so the NFD gap is unpinned. suggested_fix: Mirror attribution.py's established fix in search.py's tokenize() (line 144): normalize before matching — `return _TOKEN_RE.findall(unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text).lower())` (add `import unicodedata`). title: Suspended hyphenation ('pre- and post-deploy') leaves a trailing-hyphen query token that can never match — coverage deflated, relevance bucket drops on exactly-on-topic memories
location: _TOKEN_RE (line 66) — the [\w\-]* body permits trailing hyphens; query side is never kebab-expanded by design (_expand_kebab docstring, lines 153-172)
description: _TOKEN_RE is \w[\w\-]*, so a token may END with '-'. Standard written-English suspended hyphenation — 'pre- and post-deploy hooks', 'read- and write-paths', 'single- vs multi-tenant' — therefore yields query tokens like 'pre-'. Because queries are deliberately not kebab-expanded, 'pre-' can never match anything: a body containing 'pre-deploy' expands to {'pre-deploy','pre','deploy'}, none of which equals 'pre-'. The dead token still counts in the coverage denominator (query_unique), so a memory that is a perfect topical match ('Run DB migrations in the pre-deploy hooks; cache busting in the post-deploy hooks.') gets 2/3 coverage -> 'medium' instead of the 3/3 -> 'high' it gets when the same query is written without the suspended hyphen ('pre and post-deploy hooks' matches 'pre' via the body-side kebab expansion). The bucket drop also disables expand_top (which requires 'high') and depresses both keyword and BM25 scores. Trivial fix: strip trailing hyphens from tokens (or treat a trailing-hyphen token as its hyphenless stem on the query side). Queries arriving via memory_search are usually model-composed prose, where suspended hyphenation genuinely occurs, though terse human queries make it less frequent.
example_input: query='pre- and post-deploy hooks' against body 'Run DB migrations in the pre-deploy hooks; cache busting in the post-deploy hooks.'
expected: all three meaningful query concepts match (pre, post-deploy, hooks) -> relevance 'high'
actual: query tokens are ['pre-','post-deploy','hooks']; 'pre-' is unmatchable, so the hit reports relevance 'medium' with match_terms ['post-deploy','hooks'] (2/3 coverage)

Repro reproduces byte-for-byte: query 'pre- and post-deploy hooks' tokenizes to ['pre-', 'post-deploy', 'hooks'] and the perfect-match memory gets relevance 'medium' with match_terms ['post-deploy', 'hooks']; the same query without the suspended hyphen ('pre and post-deploy hooks') gets 'high' with all three terms matched. Confirmed in all three lexical modes (keyword, bm25, hybrid) because _build_hit (src/bettermemory/search.py:545) computes the coverage-based relevance label uniformly. Mechanism confirmed in code: _TOKEN_RE = r"\w[\w\-]*" (search.py:66) permits trailing hyphens; query tokens are never kebab-expanded (deliberate asymmetry, search.py:153-172), so 'pre-' can never equal anything in a body's expanded token set {'pre-deploy','pre','deploy'}; the dead token still counts in query_unique (search.py:871). Body side is unaffected — a body-side 'pre-' kebab-expands to include 'pre'. NOT a documented trade-off: the _TOKEN_RE comment (lines 52-66) covers unicode and kebab-wholeness only; no test pins trailing-hyphen tokens; the _expand_kebab asymmetry rationale (specific-intent compound queries) does not apply to a punctuation artifact. Downstream high-bucket gates verified: handlers/search.py:400 (expand_top requires 'high'), audit.py:466 (silent-miss probe clears_threshold = relevance == 'high' — the bug also generates false near-miss audit telemetry), eval.py:861. The FTS5 prefilter (index.py:519-522, unicode61 tokenizer, OR-joined terms)

title: Dotted-ref guard swallows genuinely dotted vendor secrets — SendGrid SG.x.y and Vault hvs. tokens rejected as 'attribute references'
location: _looks_like_secret dotted-ref branch, line 178

title: camelCase identifiers are opaque to kebab expansion — identifier-spelled facts vs prose transcripts zero-overlap and flag

title: Nested project roots: correctly-tagged child-project writes are always gated to add the parent scope

description: Pass 2 treats every (scope, root) pair independently and only skips a root when THAT scope is declared. title: origin.capture stores the symlink-RESOLVED cwd, but pass-2 does a literal find — paths spelled through the symlink (e.g. /tmp/... on macOS) never match the inferred root
location: detect_scope_mismatch pass 2 literal body.find(root) at line 176, fed by collect_project_roots (lines 222-246) consuming origin.capture's Path.cwd().resolve() (origin.py lines 107-114)
description: capture() canonicalizes the session cwd with .resolve(), which expands every symlink, so the root collect_project_roots infers is the canonical spelling. But shells, prompts, user messages, and assistant prose all use the symlinked spelling — which is what lands in memory bodies. On macOS /tmp, /var, and /etc are symlinks into /private, so any scratch checkout worked from /tmp/<proj> (a common 'cloned to /tmp to test' pattern) gets root /private/tmp/<proj> while every body cites /tmp/<proj>/... — pass 2 can never match. The same divergence hits users whose code directory is a symlink (~/code -> /Volumes/Dev/code, stow-managed trees, NFS automount /home -> /export/home). The mirror-image case also holds: a body that pastes the resolved /private/tmp spelling while cwd was captured unresolved would miss too, but capture's unconditional resolve() makes the symlink-spelled-body direction the systematic one. Result: the project-root check is silently dead for any project reached through a symlink, with no warning that the two spellings diverged.
example_input: capture(cwd=Path('/tmp/scratch-foo')) stores origin.cwd='/private/tmp/scratch-foo' (macOS /tmp symlink, no setup needed); then detect_scope_mismatch(body='Test harness for foo is /tmp/scratch-foo/run.sh — keep using it until the fix lands.', declared_scopes=['tools'], project_scopes=set(), project_roots={'projects:foo': '/private/tmp/scratch-foo'})
expected: has_mismatch=True — /tmp/scratch-foo/run.sh and /private/tmp/scratch-foo/run.sh are the same file; the citation is under projects:foo's root
actual: has_mismatch=False; the identical body spelled with the resolved /private/tmp prefix flags True
verifier_notes: Confirmed false-negative, with caveats. Repro at HEAD 874b0b0 matches the claim exactly: origin.capture stores the canonical spelling (/private/tmp/scratch-foo) and detect_scope_mismatch pass 2 (src/bettermemory/scope_match.py:176, literal body.find(root)) never matches the symlinked spelling /tmp/scratch-foo that shells and prose use. Not documented as a trade-off anywhere: the pass-2 comment (scope_match.py:164-175) covers substring/boundary concerns only; tests/test_scope_match.py doesn't pin the behavior. The codebase is demonstrably aware of the macOS /private idiom elsewhere — _git_worktree_root (origin.py:311-327) resolves both sides precisely so symlink spellings compare equal, and verify.py:360-377 (_normalize_for_compare) deliberately avoids resolve() when comparing against body text — pass 2 is the one comparison that resolves exactly one side. Two corrections to the claim: (1) .resolve() in capture() is NOT the root cause for production — capture(cwd=None) reads Path.cwd(), and POSIX getcwd is already symlink-free (verified: process in /tmp reports getcwd=/private/tmp, $PWD=/tmp), so removing resolve() fixes nothing and would break the worktree-equality contract origin.py documents; the fix must add alias matching at comparison time. (2) The repro overstates impact by passing project_scopes=set(), impossible at the production callsite (handlers/write.py:317-327 feeds both passes from the same load_all(), so any scope with an inferred root is also in project_scopes
suggested_fix: Add alias-spelling matching in pass 2 of detect_scope_mismatch (src/bettermemory/scope_match.py), keeping the literal-substring design and both boundary guards. Minimal version: for each root, build a small alias set with a pure string transform for the macOS /private idiom — if root starts with "/private/tmp/", "/private/var/", or "/private/etc/" (or equals "/private/tmp" etc.), add the spelling with the "/private" prefix stripped; symmetrically, if it starts with "/tmp/", "/var/", or "/etc/", add the "/private"-prefixed spelling. Try body.find() on each alias with the existing leading/trailing boundary checks, reporting the first hit. No filesystem calls, no existence checks, zero new false-positive surface (the aliases are by-construction equivalent spellings on macOS and implausible collisions elsewhere). Do NOT touch capture()'s resolve() — getcwd is already canonical and worktree equality (origin.py:311-327) depends on resolved spellings. Optional fuller follow-up for the general ~/code -> /Volumes case: in origin.capture(cwd=None), when os.environ.get("PWD") is set and os.path.samefile(PWD, os.getcwd()) holds, record the logical spelling as an additive cwd alias field, have collect_project_roots emit both spellings per scope, and let pass 2 try each — additive file-format change, mirrors the existing legacy-null tolerance.

title: Userless scp-form remotes (host:path/repo.git) bypass all normalization — even .git-suffix variants of the identical remote never match
location: _SSH_REMOTE_RE (line 519) requires a 'user@' prefix; _parse_remote returns None at line 552; repos_match falls back to raw string equality at lines 150-153
description: Git fully supports the userless scp-like remote form 'host:path/repo.git' — it is the natural spelling when ~/.ssh/config supplies the user via a Host alias (the standard multi-account GitHub setup: 'Host gh-work / User git', then 'git clone gh-work:owner/repo.git') or when the local username matches the server. _SSH_REMOTE_RE hard-requires '[a-zA-Z0-9_.+-]+@' before the host, and the string has no scheme, so _parse_remote returns None and repos_match degrades to raw string equality. That silently switches off EVERY normalization the function exists to provide: the .git suffix is no longer stripped (so 'gitbox:team/project.git' vs 'gitbox:team/project' — the same remote re-added without the suffix — never match), and the userless form never matches the 'git@'-prefixed or 'ssh://' spelling of the same repo. All memories written from one clone are hidden from the other.
example_input: memory_repo='gitbox:team/project.git' vs current_repo='gitbox:team/project' (same repo, .git dropped); also 'gitbox:team/project.git' vs 'git@gitbox:team/project.git' and vs 'ssh://deploy@server.example.com/repos/project.git'
expected: repos_match → True for all spellings of the same repo, as it is for every user@-prefixed/https/ssh form (the .git suffix is explicitly documented as normalized)
actual: repos_match → False for every pair; _parse_remote returns None for all userless scp-form strings, so comparison is raw string equality
verifier_notes: Confirmed, with one material correction to the claimed blast radius. Repro at HEAD 874b0b0 matches exactly: _parse_remote('gitbox:team/project.git') -> None; repos_match('gitbox:team/project.git','gitbox:team/project') -> False; repos_match('gitbox:team/project.git','git@gitbox:team/project.git') -> False. Root cause is as claimed: _SSH_REMOTE_RE (/Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/origin.py:519) hard-requires a 'user@' prefix, git's documented scp-like syntax is '[user@]host.xz:path/to/repo.git' with user optional (the standard ssh-config Host-alias multi-account setup produces exactly this form), so _parse_remote returns None (line 552) and repos_match degrades to raw string equality (lines 150-153), disabling .git-suffix and cross-spelling normalization. This is an oversight, not a documented trade-off: the regex required user@ from its introduction (commit 62cc48a, never narrowed), no docs mention the limitation, and the test comment at tests/test_origin.py:172-173 falsely asserts '"fileserver:project.git" looks SSH-like to the regex (it'll match)' — showing the author believed userless forms were handled. The conservative-fallback rationale covers 'opaque URLs', which this is not. CORRECTION to claim: 'all memories written from one clone are hidden from the other' is mostly moot — every surface-filter callsite (search.py:508, _response.py:648/692/767) passes caller_worktree_root, and separate clones have different worktree roots, so cross-clo
suggested_fix: In /Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/origin.py:519, make the user part optional and tighten the host charset so the relaxation cannot widen matching onto non-remote strings: _SSH_REMOTE_RE = re.compile(r"^(?:[a-zA-Z0-9_.+-]+@)?([^/:@]{2,}):/?([^/]+)/(.+?)(?:\.git)?/?$"). Rationale for each change: (?:...@)? matches git's documented [user@] optionality; host charset [^/:@] (was [^:]+) excludes '/' so slash-before-colon strings (which git treats as local paths, e.g. './local/path:odd') still fall through to the raw-equality fallback, and excludes '@' to keep multi-@ strings unambiguous; {2,} rejects single-letter hosts so Windows drive paths ('C:/Users/...') never parse as remotes. Verified against the existing forms: git@host:owner/repo(.git), gitbox:team/project(.git) -> identical (host,owner,name); http(s)://, ssh://, git:// still fall through to the urlparse branch (the double slash defeats the scp regex); 'weird-protocol-a', absolute paths, and 'fileserver:project.git' (no owner/name slash) still return None -> raw-equality fallback preserved. Add tests: userless-vs-userless with/without .git, userless-vs-git@-prefixed, userless-vs-ssh:// scheme of the same repo, and negative tests for 'C:/Users/foo/repo' and './local/path:odd' falling back to raw equality. Also fix the stale comment in tests/test_origin.py:172-173 which wrongly claims 'fileserver:project.git' matches the SSH regex (it does not, before or after this change — its path has no owner/name slash).

title: Home-relative vs absolute server-path spellings of one plain-SSH repo never match — git's documented-equivalent pair ssh://host/~/path and host:path parse to different (host, owner, name) triples
location: _parse_remote, SSH branch lines 529-535 and URL branch lines 537-550 — the first path segment is blindly taken as 'owner'
description: On plain-SSH hosting (a bare repo on a server, no forge), the same repo is legitimately cloned under several path spellings: 'git@server:repos/project.git' (scp form, relative to the remote user's home — the conventional form), 'ssh://git@server/~/repos/project.git' (git's own documentation lists this as the ssh:// equivalent of the scp relative form), 'git@server:~/repos/project.git' (explicit tilde), and 'git@server:/home/git/repos/project.git' (the absolute path, often what admin docs show). _parse_remote treats the first path segment as the forge 'owner', so these yield ('server','repos','project'), ('server','~','repos/project'), and ('server','home','git/repos/project') — three different identities for one repo. Memories written from a clone using one spelling are permanently hidden from a clone using another; 5 of the 6 pairings fail, including the pair git documents as equivalent.
example_input: memory_repo='git@server:repos/project.git' vs current_repo='ssh://git@server/~/repos/project.git' (or vs 'git@server:/home/git/repos/project.git')
expected: repos_match → True: all four spellings address the same bare repo on the same host, two of them by git-documented equivalence
actual: repos_match → False for every pairing except the two explicit-tilde forms; the home-dir component or '~' is compared as the 'owner'
verifier_notes: Reproduces exactly as claimed. _parse_remote in /Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/origin.py blindly takes the first path segment as forge 'owner', so 'ssh://git@server/~/repos/project.git' -> ('server','~','repos/project'), 'git@server:repos/project.git' -> ('server','repos','project'), 'git@server:/home/git/repos/project.git' -> ('server','home','git/repos/project'). Pairwise repos_match over the four spellings returns [False, True, False, False, False, False] — only the two explicit-tilde forms match. This is NOT a documented trade-off: the parsing comment block (~line 510) only claims coverage of forge forms, repos_match's docstring discusses only github-style owner/repo normalization, and tests/test_origin.py has no tilde or plain-SSH case pinning the behavior. An 'owner' of '~' is semantically absurd, so this is an oversight, not intent. The git-documented equivalence cited in the claim is real (gitcli URL docs: scp-form relative paths are home-relative, and ~[user] expansion is supported in both ssh:// and scp forms), so the tilde/relative pairings are genuine false negatives. HOWEVER the claim is overbroad on the absolute-path pairings: equating 'git@server:/home/git/repos/project.git' with the home-relative forms is not decidable client-side (requires knowing the remote user's home dir) and equating them heuristically would risk exactly the false-positive collisions the module documents failing closed against — so 2 of the 5 'broken' pair
suggested_fix: In _parse_remote (src/bettermemory/origin.py, lines 522-550), normalize a bare leading home-tilde before the owner/name split, in both branches. Concretely: in the SSH-regex branch, reconstruct the full remote path (owner + '/' + name), apply path = path.removeprefix('~/'), then re-split on the first '/'; in the ssh:// URL branch, apply path = path.removeprefix('~/') after path.strip('/') and before the '/'-presence check. If stripping '~/' leaves a path with no '/', return None so repos_match falls back to raw string equality (fail-closed, consistent with the existing unparseable-URL fallback). Do NOT attempt to equate absolute server paths (/home/git/...) with home-relative ones — that equivalence is undecidable client-side and matching it heuristically would introduce the false positives the module's design explicitly avoids. Add tests: git@server:repos/project.git == git@server:~/repos/project.git == ssh://git@server/~/repos/project.git all mutually match; git@server:/home/git/repos/project.git still matches none of them; git@server:~/project.git (no second segment after stripping) falls back to raw-string equality.

title: Push-mirror setup (git remote set-url --add origin <mirror>) flips capture() to the LAST configured URL — the day a mirror is added, every previously written memory for the repo goes invisible
location: _git_remote_url, lines 297-298 ('git config --get remote.origin.url')
description: The canonical recipe for pushing one repo to two remotes (GitHub + GitLab mirroring, ubiquitous in blog posts and SO answers) is 'git remote set-url --add origin <mirror-url>', which makes remote.origin.url multi-valued. Verified: 'git config --get' on a multi-valued key returns the LAST value with exit 0 — the mirror — while fetch and 'git remote get-url origin' use the FIRST (canonical) URL. So from the moment the mirror is added, capture() records the mirror's URL on every write and search, while all memories written before that day carry the canonical URL. repos_match across the two hosts is False, so the entire pre-mirror history of the project is silently hidden in the very checkout that wrote it (and post-mirror writes are likewise invisible to any mirror-less clone of the same repo). Distinct from the already-reported insteadOf finding: no URL rewriting/aliases are involved — both values are plain literal URLs; the bug is that --get's last-value semantics select the non-fetch URL.
example_input: A checkout where the user ran: git remote set-url --add origin git@gitlab.com:owner/repo-mirror.git (original origin url git@github.com:owner/repo.git); memories written before that command carry repo='git@github.com:owner/repo.git'
expected: capture() records the repo's canonical fetch URL (what 'git remote get-url origin' returns — the first value), so pre- and post-mirror memories keep matching
actual: capture() records 'git@gitlab.com:owner/repo-mirror.git' (last value); repos_match('git@github.com:owner/repo.git', 'git@gitlab.com:owner/repo-mirror.git') → False; all earlier memories stop surfacing
verifier_notes: Confirmed end-to-end on git 2.50.1 (Apple Git-155). (1) In a repo with `git remote add origin git@github.com:owner/repo.git` followed by `git remote set-url --add origin git@gitlab.com:owner/repo-mirror.git`, `git config --get remote.origin.url` returns the LAST value (the gitlab mirror) with exit 0, while `git remote get-url origin` and the fetch line of `git remote -v` use the FIRST (canonical github) URL. (2) `capture()` (src/bettermemory/origin.py, _git_remote_url at lines 297-298) therefore records the mirror URL; `repos_match('git@github.com:owner/repo.git', 'git@gitlab.com:owner/repo-mirror.git')` is False (different host AND name), and `should_include_for_caller` returns False even with identical worktree_root — so every pre-mirror memory is hidden from auto-scoped memory_search/memory_scope_overview in the very checkout that wrote it, and post-mirror writes are invisible to mirror-less clones. (3) Not a documented trade-off: origin.py's docstring and the parsing comment at line 513 presume single-valued output; tests/test_origin.py only covers the no-remote case (line 95); no mention of multi-valued remotes/insteadOf/set-url anywhere in src, tests, or CHANGELOG. Decisive evidence it's an oversight, not a design choice: sync.py:382 in the same codebase already uses the correct `git remote get-url origin` idiom. (4) Genuinely distinct from the prior insteadOf finding — both URLs here are literal, no rewriting; the bug is --get's last-value semantics selecting the non-f
suggested_fix: In src/bettermemory/origin.py change _git_remote_url (lines 297-298) from `_git(cwd, "config", "--get", "remote.origin.url")` to `_git(cwd, "remote", "get-url", "origin")` — this returns the first (canonical fetch) URL, is available since git 2.7 (2016), preserves the swallow-failures contract (`_git` already maps non-zero exit such as "No such remote" to None), and matches the idiom the codebase already uses at sync.py:382. Update the stale comment at origin.py:513 and the test comment at tests/test_origin.py:95, and add a regression test that builds a repo with `git remote set-url --add origin <mirror>` and asserts capture() returns the first URL. One caveat to record in the commit message: `git remote get-url` applies url.<base>.insteadOf rewriting where `config --get` returns the raw value — that change is in the same direction as the separately-reported insteadOf finding (the rewritten URL is what fetch actually uses), but if raw-config semantics must be preserved for that finding's resolution, the alternative minimal fix is `_git(cwd, "config", "--get-all", "remote.origin.url")` and take the first line. Either fix is forward-only: memories already written with the mirror URL will still mismatch the canonical URL until re-verified/updated — worth a one-line note in the CHANGELOG.

title: Proactive-capture turns self-flag: a memory written THIS turn is probed as if it were retrievable, and `write` events don't shield the verdict
location: probe_for_miss verdict branch + _RETRIEVAL_EVENT_KINDS (lines ~96, ~461-493); store snapshot taken post-turn in handlers/audit_turn.py:122 and hook.py:230
description: The probe runs over the store as it exists AFTER the turn completes (store.load_all() at audit time), so a memory the model wrote seconds earlier in the same turn is a probe candidate. Memory bodies routinely echo the user's phrasing (the write reflex captures 'we switched the staging deploys to blue-green' as 'Staging deploys switched to blue-green.'), so the just-written memory scores 'high' coverage against the very message that prompted it. Meanwhile _RETRIEVAL_EVENT_KINDS is only {search, show, list} — the `write` (and `write_confirm`) event sitting squarely inside the lookback window does not shield. Result: every turn where the model does exactly what the proactive-write contract demands (capture a NEW durable fact without a pointless search) emits a `search_miss`, with the just-created memory as the 'evidence'. The hit could not have been retrieved when the user message arrived because it did not exist yet — both Memory.created and `now` are available in probe_for_miss to exclude it, and the write event is available to shield, but neither is consulted. In-project suppression does not rescue the common cases: global facts (infrastructure/tools scopes), writes from non-repo cwds, and remoteless repos all bypass it. This poisons the silent-miss telemetry with the system's flagship good behavior.
example_input: User: 'we switched the staging deploys to blue-green'. Model writes Memory(body='Staging deploys switched to blue-green.', scopes=['infrastructure']) 20s before the Stop-hook audit; event log contains the kind='write' event 18s ago in the same session; no search this turn (correct — the fact is new).
expected: verdict='ok' (or 'no_signal'): nothing was missed — the only high-relevance hit was created by this very turn, and the model demonstrably engaged with the memory store via the write.
actual: verdict='miss', recent_retrieval_count=0, search_miss event emitted with the just-written memory as top hit at relevance='high'.
verifier_notes: Confirmed, attempted refutation failed on all fronts. (1) Repro reproduces exactly at HEAD 874b0b0: verdict='miss', recent_retrieval_count=0, top hit = the just-written memory at relevance='high'. (2) Mechanism verified in code: _RETRIEVAL_EVENT_KINDS (src/bettermemory/audit.py:96) is {search, show, list}; handlers/write.py emits only kind='write'/'write_confirm' events (lines 613, 709), so a proactive-capture turn has no shield. Both audit producers snapshot the store post-turn with no created-time filter (handlers/audit_turn.py:122, hook.py:230), and the verdict branch (audit.py:461-493) never consults Memory.created — a memory that did not exist when the user message arrived is treated as retrievable evidence of a miss. (3) Not a documented trade-off: the module docstring's design notes, the handler's explicit 'Known v1 limitations' list (audit_turn.py:84-97), CHANGELOG, and the test suite (no test covers same-turn writes) are all silent on this; the _RETRIEVAL_EVENT_KINDS comment's exclusion rationale ('downstream of an earlier retrieval') does not apply to write. (4) Realistic: the server's own instructions make no-search proactive writes a routine reflex, and bodies echo user phrasing (coverage >= 0.75 -> 'high'). I verified the realistic in-repo flow: a global-scope ('infrastructure') memory written from the caller's own repo still flags 'miss', while the identical 'projects:'-scoped memory is suppressed by _caller_in_top_hit_project — exactly the suppression gap claim
suggested_fix: In probe_for_miss (src/bettermemory/audit.py), exclude memories that did not exist when the user message arrived, before run_search executes. After the now-coercion (line ~381), add: `cutoff = now - timedelta(seconds=lookback_seconds); memories = [m for m in memories if (ensure_utc(m.created) or now) <= cutoff]` (ensure_utc and timedelta are already imported; the lookback window is already the module's established proxy for "this turn" in _count_recent_retrievals). Filter on `created` only, not `updated` — an updated memory existed before and its prior content was retrievable. If the filter empties the list, the existing empty-hits path returns 'no_signal' with probe_query set, matching the documented report semantics. This is preferable to adding 'write' to _RETRIEVAL_EVENT_KINDS, which would mask genuine misses (model writes about X while a stored Y was the real unretrieved high hit) and contradict the module's documented don't-double-shield discipline — the created-time filter removes exactly the hit that could not have been retrieved while leaving older high-relevance hits free to flag correctly. Add a regression test mirroring the repro (memory created inside the lookback window, kind='write' event in window, no retrieval events -> verdict != 'miss'), plus a control asserting an OLD high-relevance memory alongside a same-turn write still flags 'miss'.

title: Concurrent sessions hijack the retrieval-shield anchor: _latest_in_process_session picks whichever process wrote last, flipping the verdict both ways
location: _latest_in_process_session (~lines 423-440) feeding probe_for_miss(retrieval_session_id=...) at hook.py ~252-258; consumed by audit.py _count_recent_retrievals (~550-584)
description: The Stop hook bridges its transcript session id to the live server session by taking the session of the MOST RECENT non-stop-hook event in the shared event log. The store and event log are shared across ALL projects and processes (that is the design), so with two concurrent Claude Code windows, a parallel worktree agent fan-out, or a cron/CLI invocation (bettermemory consolidate's Recorder writes under its own session id), the latest event frequently belongs to the OTHER session. The shield in audit.py then filters retrieval events by the wrong session id. False-positive direction: window A's model searched 10s ago (sess_A), window B's server wrote any event 5s ago (even a session-start scope_overview) -> anchor=sess_B -> sess_A's search is invisible -> recent_retrieval_count=0 -> search_miss emitted for a turn that searched correctly. False-negative direction (same root cause, verified in the same repro): only sess_B searched (an unrelated query from the other window) -> its search shields sess_A's genuine miss -> verdict 'ok'. Note events already carry a worktree_root stamp (events.py Recorder line ~232) that could disambiguate the anchor, but it is ignored. The same hijacked anchor also drives _disabled_scopes_from_events, so another window's scope toggles leak into this window's probe exclusions.
example_input: Shared event log: {'session':'sess_A','kind':'search','ts': now-10s} (this window's model searched for the topic) followed by {'session':'sess_B','kind':'scope_overview','ts': now-5s} (second Claude Code window starting up). Hook audits user message 'check pgbouncer connection pooling' against a memory 'Postgres connection pooling goes through pgbouncer on port 6432.'
expected: Anchor resolves to the session that serves THIS window's model (sess_A); its 10s-old search shields the verdict -> 'ok'. Conversely an unrelated session's search must not shield this window's miss.
actual: Anchor=sess_B; verdict='miss' with recent_retrieval_count=0 despite the in-window search by sess_A. In the mirrored setup (only sess_B searched), verdict='ok' with recent_retrieval_count=1 — a real miss swallowed by another process's search.
verifier_notes: CONFIRMED. Repro runs verbatim and flips the verdict both ways. (1) Mechanism verified: _latest_in_process_session (hook.py:434-440) anchors to the most recent non-stop-hook event's session with no worktree/process discrimination; _count_recent_retrievals (audit.py:578) filters by strict session equality, so the shield sees only the hijacking session's retrievals. The same anchor drives _disabled_scopes_from_events (hook.py:401) and _emit_hook_attributions (hook.py:475), so scope-toggle leakage and attribution misses ride the same defect. (2) Partially documented, but the documentation is wrong in the direction that matters: hook.py docstring lines 49-58 acknowledges concurrent sessions only for disabled-scope attribution, claims the bias is suppress-only, and assumes 'single-active-server deployment' — while docs/ROADMAP.md:17 advertises hardened 'concurrent multi-agent store access'. The false-positive direction (spurious search_miss for a turn that searched correctly) is undocumented and breaks the audit's conservative design. No test covers concurrent sessions for this anchor (only the sequential restart-gap, test_hook.py:1433). (3) Plausible, not contrived: store defaults to one global ~/.bettermemory across all projects (config.py:522); a session-start scope_overview is recorded (handlers/scope_overview.py:241) and is the user's documented session-start ritual, so opening a second window mid-turn of the first is the exact repro shape; cron/CLI 'bettermemory consolidate'
suggested_fix: Make the anchor worktree-aware using the stamp that already exists. In hook.py run_audit, pass the already-captured caller_origin.worktree_root (hook.py:236) into _latest_in_process_session; inside it, first walk reversed(events) for the latest non-stop-hook event whose event.get("worktree_root") matches the hook's worktree_root, and only if no stamped match exists fall back to the current latest-any-session behavior (preserves legacy unstamped logs and the documented reset-on-restart semantics). The server-side Recorder already stamps worktree_root on every in-process event (builder.py:142, events.py:231-232), so no write-path change is needed. Apply the same anchored helper to _disabled_scopes_from_events and _emit_hook_attributions (they already share it, so the one-helper change heals all three consumers). Update the hook.py 'Residual divergence' docstring: the concurrent-session case narrows to same-worktree concurrent sessions and the over-flagging direction should be named explicitly. Add two regression tests mirroring the repro: foreign-session event after this worktree's search must not unshield (verdict ok), and a foreign session's search must not shield this worktree's miss (verdict miss).

title: Bare numeric continuation replies ('3.8.0', 'option 2') defeat the no-signal gate via digit fragmentation and score 'high' against unrelated digit-bearing memories
location: probe_for_miss MIN_PROBE_CONTENT_TOKENS gate (~line 401, constant ~line 124); tokenizer _TOKEN_RE in search.py:66 splits on '.'
description: MIN_PROBE_CONTENT_TOKENS exists precisely to drop bare continuations ('yes', 'go for it') because the v1 coverage rule structurally labels short-query matches 'high'. But tokenize() splits dotted version strings on '.', so the canonical numeric continuation — the user answering the assistant's question with just a version string — fragments into multiple digit pseudo-tokens: '3.8.0' -> ['3','8','0'] = 3 'content tokens', sailing past the gate. Each bare digit then matches ANY memory whose body contains the same digit groups after its own dotted versions fragment (version pins, ports, cron specs are ubiquitous in memory bodies), so coverage hits 3/3 = 'high' on completely unrelated memories. title: Cold-scope pass keys only on `created`: a scope actively maintained via memory_update/memory_verify is flagged 'consider archiving' although its memory was rewritten 2 days ago

description: The cold-scope detector defines scope freshness as the newest CREATED timestamp. title: _PREFERENCE_RE requires subject-verb adjacency: any modal, adverb, or negation between 'I'/'we' and the verb silently drops canonical preference statements
location: _PREFERENCE_RE (lines 91-97), applied in extract_proposals (line 315)
description: The preference alternation is written as literal bigrams: 'i (prefer|like|love|hate|avoid|always|never|usually|want|need|use)', 'i'?m using', 'we (use|prefer|avoid|always|never)', "we'?re using". Any single token between the subject and the verb breaks the match, so the most common real phrasings of exactly the content this extractor exists to capture are never proposed: contractions/modals ("I'd prefer", "I would prefer", "I'd rather"), intensity/frequency adverbs ("I really like", "I typically use", "I generally prefer", "I mostly use", "I tend to avoid"), and negation ("I don't use", "I don't like" — note 'i hate' is a marker but the far more common 'i don't like' is not). Unless the sentence happens to contain 'my '/'our ' (itself slated for tightening per the bare-my finding), these durable preferences are silently lost — the write-reflex gap the module exists to close stays open for the most natural phrasings.

title: Dedup is queue-membership only — a dismissed (or accepted) proposal's sentence is re-proposed the very next time it recurs, turning 'a bad proposal costs one dismissal' into one dismissal per recurrence

description: The source_excerpt dedup set is derived solely from rows currently in .write_proposals.jsonl. title: CJK memory bodies tokenize as one giant clause-length token — every realistic CJK query returns zero hits in all rankers AND the FTS5 index
location: tokenize / _TOKEN_RE (~line 66, 144-150); same failure in index.py FTS5 tokenize='unicode61' (index.py ~line 141)
description: _TOKEN_RE (r'\w[\w\-]*') splits only on non-word characters. Japanese, Chinese, and Thai prose has no inter-word whitespace, so an entire clause becomes ONE token: '東京オフィスは2026年に移転する予定' tokenizes to a single 34-char token. Token matching is exact equality, so every realistic query ('東京', '移転', even the multi-word '東京オフィス') scores zero against it — keyword, bm25, and hybrid all return zero hits; the only query that can ever hit the memory is the byte-exact full clause. The FTS5 index path has the identical defect: unicode61 treats CJK codepoints as token characters, so MATCH '"東京"' returns 0 rows against the same body (verified). The module docstring explicitly claims the \w-based regex fixed 'non-English memories effectively unsearchable' — true for European scripts but the fix does not reach unsegmented scripts: a CJK-language user's memories are written successfully, pass dedup, and are then silently unretrievable forever, with no error anywhere. (Distinct from the reported NFD combining-mark and diacritic-folding findings, which are European-script codepoint issues, and from the groundedness.py CJK finding, which is a different module/heuristic.)
