title: Reduplicated phrase queries ('end to end', 'step by step', 'side by side') double-count the repeated token — an off-topic kebab-expansion match outranks the on-topic memory 2:1
location: score_memory token loop (~line 394-401); score_memory_bm25 token loop (~line 337-356) — neither dedups query_tokens before accumulating
description: Stopword stripping turns common English reduplicated phrases into a repeated token: 'end to end testing' -> ['end','end','testing'], 'step by step migration guide' -> ['step','step','migration','guide'], 'side by side comparison' -> ['side','side','comparison'] (verified). Both scoring loops iterate the RAW query token list — `for tok in query_tokens` — re-adding the full body_hits/scope contribution on each duplicate occurrence, while the `matched`/coverage bookkeeping correctly dedups via `seen`. So the repeated word's weight is silently doubled relative to every other query term. In bm25 the duplicate re-adds the entire saturated TF contribution (and the 2*idf scope bonus), defeating TF saturation from the query side. Demonstrated consequence: for query 'end to end testing', a memory 'The front-end build uses Vite' — which matches only 'end', and only via kebab expansion of 'front-end' — scores 1.6075, exactly double the genuinely on-topic 'Prefers pytest for integration testing of the handlers' (0.8037), and takes rank 1. Without the duplication the two would tie and recency/coverage would decide. score_memory(m, ['end','testing']) vs (m, ['end','end','testing']) confirms the doubling affects only the duplicated term.
example_input: Query 'end to end testing' against memory A 'Prefers pytest for integration testing of the handlers' and memory B 'The front-end build uses Vite' (same age, same scopes)
expected: A (about testing) ranks at or above B (a front-end build note that merely contains the substring token 'end'); at minimum the repeated query word counts once like every other term
actual: B ranks first at exactly 2x A's score (1.6075 vs 0.8037) because the duplicated 'end' token re-adds B's body contribution; score_memory with deduped tokens ['end','testing'] gives B 0.8037 (tie)
verifier_notes: Confirmed, and broader than claimed: the inversion holds not just in keyword mode but in bm25 (1.4324 vs 0.7715) and in the DEFAULT hybrid mode (0.0328 vs 0.0323) used by the MCP handler (handlers/search.py:155 resolves to 'hybrid'), because both fused lexical rankers double-count identically and RRF preserves the per-ranker order. Root cause verified: search() strips stopwords from the query (search.py:850) without deduping, so 'end to end testing' -> ['end','end','testing']; both score_memory (loop at search.py:394-401) and score_memory_bm25 (loop at search.py:337-356) iterate the raw list and re-add the full body/scope contribution per duplicate, while the matched/coverage bookkeeping correctly treats tokens as a set. score_memory(b,['end','end','testing']) is exactly 2x score_memory(b,['end','testing']). NOT a documented trade-off — four pieces of evidence show the design intends set semantics for query tokens: coverage divides by len(set(query_tokens)) (line 408); matched/seen dedup in both loops; the semantic path already passes list(dict.fromkeys(query_tokens)) (lines 918, 965); and the BM25 header comment (lines 232-236) explicitly criticizes the keyword scorer for 'overvaluing repeated common' terms and credits BM25's TF saturation for clipping repeats — which the raw query loop defeats from the query side (linear qtf, no saturation). test_bm25_matched_terms_deduplicated pins only matched_terms (asserts score > 0), so no test locks in the doubling. Plausibility is hi
suggested_fix: Dedup the query tokens at the top of both scorer loops, preserving order, using the idiom the module already uses for the semantic fallback: in score_memory (src/bettermemory/search.py:394) and score_memory_bm25 (src/bettermemory/search.py:337) change `for tok in query_tokens:` to `for tok in dict.fromkeys(query_tokens):`. This is behavior-preserving for all non-duplicated queries (scores byte-identical), leaves matched_terms and coverage semantics unchanged (both already dedup via seen/set), and fixes all exported direct callers of the scorers — safer than deduping only in search() at line 850, since the module docstring advertises the per-mode scorers for direct wiring. Add a regression test asserting score_memory(m, ['end','end','testing'], now=now) == score_memory(m, ['end','testing'], now=now) and the bm25 equivalent, plus an end-to-end test that 'end to end testing' ranks a testing memory at or above a front-end memory of equal age.

title: Retrieval-meta filler words ('remember', 'know', 'anything', 'stored', 'about', 'tell') are not stopwords — natural 'free text' retrieval queries deflate an exactly-on-topic memory to relevance 'low' (= documented 'probable noise')
location: _STOPWORDS (~line 78-141) feeding _relevance_label coverage (~line 179-193) via query_unique in search() (~line 871)
description: The relevance bucket is matched_unique/query_unique over stopword-stripped query tokens, and the stoplist covers only grammatical filler (articles, pronouns, auxiliaries). The words that frame virtually every natural retrieval question — 'remember', 'know', 'tell', 'anything', 'stored', 'about', 'saved' — all survive stripping and inflate query_unique without ever being matchable. The MCP tool description documents `query` as 'free text' and instructs the model to 'treat low as probable noise', so the bucket is load-bearing. Verified: against the memory 'Prefers a rebase-heavy git workflow with small atomic commits', query 'git workflow' is high, but the natural phrasing 'do you remember anything stored about the preferred git workflow' yields 7 unique tokens of which only git+workflow can match -> coverage 2/7 = 0.29 -> 'low' on the exactly-on-topic top hit (and 'what do you know about the user's preferred git workflow' likewise -> 'low'). The same deflation disarms expand_top (requires 'high'). Distinct from the reported fragment ('s','t') and stopword-homograph findings: those are over-stripping/fragment bugs; this is systematic under-stripping of the retrieval-meta vocabulary the tool's own contract invites ('Do you remember...' phrasings). Borderline-by-design (the stoplist is documented as deliberately short), but the measured effect — the canonical retrieval phrasing labeling the right answer 'probable noise' — is a concrete false signal.
example_input: Query 'do you remember anything stored about the preferred git workflow' against memory 'Prefers a rebase-heavy git workflow with small atomic commits'
expected: The only on-topic memory, matching both content words of the question, is labeled high (or at least medium) relevance
actual: relevance='low' (coverage 2/7: 'remember', 'anything', 'stored', 'about', 'preferred' all count as unmatched query terms); tool description tells the model to treat 'low' as probable noise, and expand_top will not fire
verifier_notes: VERIFIED. Repro run at HEAD 874b0b0 (hybrid mode, no embeddings): 'git workflow' -> relevance='high'; 'do you remember anything stored about the preferred git workflow' -> relevance='low', match_terms=['git','workflow'] on the exactly-on-topic memory. Mechanics confirmed in /Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/search.py: query_unique = len(set(_strip_stopwords(tokenize(query)))) (lines 850/871), relevance = matched/query_unique with low < 0.40 (_relevance_label, lines 179-193); _STOPWORDS (78-141) contains no retrieval-meta vocabulary. Crucially, the deflation stands on retrieval-meta words ALONE, independent of the separately-reported 's'-fragment and no-stemming issues: 'do you remember anything stored about git workflow' survives as [remember, anything, stored, about, git, workflow] -> 2/6 = 0.33 -> 'low'. Attempted refutations failed: (a) the stoplist comment's documented rationale ("domain words get/set/run stay in") does not cover 'about' (preposition — at/by/of/on/in/with/for/from are all listed) or 'anything' (indefinite pronoun — it/me/us/them/they/these are listed); those are omissions within the list's own taxonomy, not deliberate keeps. (b) The only in-tree acknowledgment of natural-language coverage deflation (audit.py docstring lines 55-57: "multi-token natural language with stopwords often lands at 2/3 = medium") acknowledges 'medium', not an exact-topic match labeled 'low'. (c) The 'honest retrieval signals' changelog/3.4.x decision
suggested_fix: Two-part minimal fix preserving the documented conservative design in /Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/search.py: (1) Add the pure grammatical omissions to _STOPWORDS (lines 78-141): 'about', 'anything' (optionally 'something', 'everything') — same word classes as existing entries (prepositions, indefinite pronouns), so the existing 'domain words stay in' rationale is untouched. (2) For the retrieval-meta verbs ('remember', 'recall', 'know', 'tell', 'stored', 'saved', 'said'), which carry mild domain-word risk on the body side (e.g. a memory body 'credentials stored in 1Password' should keep 'stored' in its BM25/IDF and dedup statistics), introduce a small _QUERY_META_WORDS frozenset stripped ONLY at the query-side strip in search() (line ~850, alongside _strip_stopwords) so they vanish from both matching and the query_unique denominator (line 871) while compute_idf (line 275), score_memory_bm25 (line 323) and _content_token_set (line 1015) body tokenization stay byte-identical. This mirrors the query-vs-index asymmetry already documented on _expand_kebab (lines 153-164). Add a regression test next to test_stopwords_stripped_but_real_terms_still_match in tests/test_search.py: exact-topic memory + query 'do you remember anything stored about <both content words>' asserts relevance == 'high' (6 tokens reduce to 2/2 after the fix). Optionally also fix the now-stale half of the comment at lines 72-73 ('bodies stay unfiltered') which compute_idf/score_memory_bm25 already contradict.

title: 'recently' — the most common recent-action adverb — slips the gate entirely while 'i just'/'we just' fire
location: TRANSIENT_PHRASE_MARKERS, 'Recent-action references' section (lines 64-69); matched via find_transient_markers (lines 145-166)
description: The 'Recent-action references' marker section only covers first-person bigrams ('i just', 'we just') and the 'shipped' pair ('just shipped', 'shipped today'). The same statement phrased in first person ('We just switched...') is rejected, so the gate's behavior depends on grammatical person rather than transience.

expected: A transient_warning hit (recent-action reference: 'recently switched' and 'caches are stale' will be meaningless in a week), same as the equivalent 'We just switched from yarn to pnpm.' which fires 'we just'.
actual: find_transient_markers returns [] — the body commits with no warning. 'The default branch was recently renamed from master to main.' also returns []. The contrast body 'We just switched from yarn to pnpm.' fires marker 'we just'.

Add parametrized positive tests ('The team recently switched from yarn to pnpm', 'The default branch was recently renamed') and negative tests ('evicts the least-recently-used entry', 'the Recently Viewed panel') to tests/test_durability.py. title: Time-word product/title homonyms fire 'tomorrow' and 'this week' on durable infra and preference facts (tomorrow.io API, Tomorrow Night theme, This Week in Rust)
location: TRANSIENT_PHRASE_MARKERS 'tomorrow' (line 60) and 'this week' (line 61); case-insensitive \b match in _PHRASE_REGEXES (lines 100-103)

title: git-describe version strings (v3.7.1-5-g874b0b0) defeat the SHA detector — the g-prefix removes the \b, so the canonical machine-generated branch-state string slips
location: _SHA_RE (line 94: r"\b(?=[0-9a-f]*[a-f])[0-9a-f]{7,40}\b"); SHA loop in find_transient_markers (lines 168-181)
description: `git describe` output — the standard way build/deploy tooling stamps 'where the tree is' — embeds the abbreviated commit hash with a literal 'g' prefix: v3.7.1-5-g874b0b0. Since 'g' is a word character outside [0-9a-f], there is no \b between 'g' and the hex run, so _SHA_RE never matches and the regex cannot backtrack into the run's interior. The exact same SHA written bare ('at 874b0b0') fires sha:874b0b0. Bodies like 'The deployed build is v3.7.1-5-g874b0b0' are pure branch state (N commits past a tag — stale on the next deploy), i.e. precisely the 'you're putting branch state in memory' signal the SHA bucket exists to raise, in its single most common machine-generated spelling. Notably this very repo's HEAD would describe as v3.8.0-g874b0b0-style output, so the shape appears in real release/deploy notes for this project.
example_input: The deployed build is v3.7.1-5-g874b0b0, two commits past the release tag.
expected: A sha:874b0b0 transient hit — identical commit-state information to the bare-SHA spelling 'The deployed build is at 874b0b0, ...', which does fire.
actual: find_transient_markers returns [] for the git-describe form (and for 'image tagged 2.4.0-12-ge9a3f1c'); the body commits as durable. The bare-SHA contrast body fires ['sha:874b0b0'].
verifier_notes: Confirmed false-negative. Mechanics check out: _SHA_RE (src/bettermemory/durability.py:94) anchors on \b, and the 'g' in git-describe output (v3.7.1-5-g874b0b0) is a word character outside [0-9a-f], so no word boundary exists at or inside the hex run — the regex cannot match at any position. The bare-SHA spelling of the same fact fires sha:874b0b0. Not a documented trade-off: the design comment (lines 82-93) enumerates the trade-offs it accepted (7-char lower bound, 40-char upper bound, lowercase-only, a-f lookahead vs decimals) and tests/test_durability.py pins each of those negatives — neither mentions the g-prefix/describe form, and grep finds no describe handling anywhere in src/tests/docs (file history is two commits, neither touching this). Real-world plausible: git describe is the canonical machine spelling of branch state (CI stamps, --version strings, image tags), and this repo's own HEAD describes as v3.8.0-1-g6fb74d2 right now — the exact claimed shape. Compounding: the natural prose around such strings ('two commits past the release tag') matches neither 'commits ahead' nor 'commits behind', so the whole branch-state body commits durable with zero signal. Severity medium per rubric: realistic but occasional — most transient bodies still trip a phrase marker or bare SHA; this gap bites only when the describe string is the sole marker. Gate is used at handlers/write.py:287, proposals.py:326, consolidate.py:1582.
suggested_fix:
Keep _SHA_RE untouched and add one describe-specific pattern in src/bettermemory/durability.py, since '-g<hex>' is uniquely the git-describe spelling (the tag-N-gSHA form always carries the dash, covering both claimed examples):

_DESCRIBE_SHA_RE = re.compile(r"(?<=-g)(?=[0-9a-f]*[a-f])[0-9a-f]{7,40}\b")

In find_transient_markers, scan both patterns in the existing SHA loop, e.g. `for match in itertools.chain(_SHA_RE.finditer(content), _DESCRIBE_SHA_RE.finditer(content)):` — the existing `if "sha" in seen: break` bucketing already collapses everything to one hit, and the lookbehind keeps match.group() as the bare hex so the `sha:<7-char prefix>` marker format is unchanged. Probe-tested an equivalent pattern against every pinned negative case (6-char hex, all-decimal epochs/phones/ids, uppercase ULID, 41-char hex blob, English g-words): zero new fires — the conservative design's false-positive budget is untouched. Add two tests mirroring the claimed inputs: 'The deployed build is v3.7.1-5-g874b0b0...' fires sha:874b0b0; 'image tagged 2.4.0-12-ge9a3f1c' fires sha:e9a3f1c.

title: PEM detector fires on key-format documentation prose — the header line alone, with no key material, blocks the write
location: _PREFIXED_DETECTORS, 'private-key-pem' entry, lines 97-100
description: The PEM detector matches only the literal header string '-----BEGIN (RSA |EC |DSA |OPENSSH |PGP )?PRIVATE KEY-----' with no requirement that any base64 key material follows. Durable tooling notes routinely QUOTE the header to describe a key FORMAT (the exact 'describe credentials without containing them' case): e.g. 'Paramiko < 2.7 cannot read the new OpenSSH key format (files begin <defanged:private-key-pem>); convert with ssh-keygen -p -m PEM' or 'GitLab CI's SSH_PRIVATE_KEY must be PEM, i.e. start with <defanged:private-key-pem>'. Such bodies contain zero secret bytes yet are blocked, training the rubber-stamp override the module docstring warns about. The placeholder machinery (_PLACEHOLDER_VALUES, env-template guards) is consulted only by the generic rule, so prefixed detectors have no escape hatch; a cheap fix is to require the header be followed by a newline plus a base64-looking line (the module's own _safe_snippet comment assumes 'the bytes AFTER the match are raw key material', which is false for doc prose).
example_input: Paramiko < 2.7 cannot read the new OpenSSH key format (files begin '<defanged:private-key-pem>'); convert with ssh-keygen -p -m PEM.
expected: [] — the body documents a file-format header; there is no private key in it
actual: [CredentialMatch(kind='private-key-pem', ...)] — write blocked with credential_warning
verifier_notes: Confirmed, despite the default-refute stance. (1) Repro reproduces verbatim at HEAD 874b0b0: find_credential_markers on the Paramiko doc-prose body returns [CredentialMatch(kind='private-key-pem', snippet="...ey format (files begin '[redacted:private-key-pem]...")] — memory_write would reject with credential_warning. (2) This is not a documented trade-off: the detector comment (src/bettermemory/credentials.py:95-96, "One match is enough to flag 'you pasted a private key'") and the _safe_snippet docstring (lines 254-258, "the bytes AFTER the match are raw key material, not context") both REST on the assumption that the header only appears when a key was pasted — neither acknowledges prose that quotes the header. The module's own contract (lines 28-31: "a memory body that merely *mentions* … as prose must never fire; a false positive … trains the user to rubber-stamp the override") classifies this behavior as a defect by the project's own standard. (3) No escape hatch: CredentialGate (src/bettermemory/handlers/write.py:244-248, also handlers/update.py:181) feeds the raw body to the detector; _PLACEHOLDER_VALUES/_looks_like_secret gate only the generic keyword rule, exactly as claimed. (4) No test pins the prose case as intended — tests/test_credentials.py's negative section covers only generic-rule prose; positive PEM fixtures (lines 124, 209-222) all include base64 key material after the header, so the suggested fix breaks no pinned behavior. (5) Plausibility: the example bodi
suggested_fix:
In src/bettermemory/credentials.py, _PREFIXED_DETECTORS 'private-key-pem' entry (lines 97-100): require the header to be followed by an end-of-line and a line that looks like key material or a PEM encapsulation header — a real paste always has this; prose quoting the header never does. Replace the pattern with:

    (
        "private-key-pem",
        # Header must be followed by a line of base64 key material (or a
        # Proc-Type:/DEK-Info: encapsulation header for encrypted traditional
        # PEM). Prose that merely QUOTES the header to describe a key format
        # ("files begin '<defanged:private-key-pem>'") must not fire.
        re.compile(
            r"-----BEGIN (?:RSA |EC |DSA |OPENSSH |PGP )?PRIVATE KEY-----"
            r"(?=[ \t]*\r?\n(?:[A-Za-z0-9+/=_-]{16,}|(?:Proc-Type|DEK-Info):))"
        ),
    ),

Verified against existing positive fixtures (tests/test_credentials.py:124 header+base64 line, and lines 209-222 full key block) — both still fire — and against all three prose shapes (Paramiko note, GitLab CI note, backtick-quoted header) — none fire. The lookahead is zero-width so match.end() stays at the header end, keeping the _safe_snippet 'private-key-pem' trailing-window suppression (line 260) and redaction behavior unchanged, and making its lines 254-258 comment ("bytes AFTER the match are raw key material") actually true. Add two regression tests: a negative test in the prose section asserting find_credential_markers returns [] for the Paramiko/GitLab doc-prose bodies, and keep a positive paste case. This preserves the module's documented precision-over-recall tripwire design (docstring lines 28-35): any paste with actual key material still fires; a bare header with no key carries no secret to protect.

title: Digit-less passphrases (diceware/memorable style) never fire the generic rule — has_digit is a hard requirement
location: _looks_like_secret, lines 187-189 (has_alpha and has_digit)
description: _looks_like_secret returns False unless the value contains at least one digit ('a literal secret mixes character classes'). But the canonical human-memorable password shape — diceware / 1Password 'memorable' style word chains like 'orbit-mango-velvet-cactus-flame' — is long, high-diversity, and letters-only. 'remember: the family iCloud password is orbit-mango-velvet-cactus-flame' sails through every detector and the secret lands in plaintext markdown, .events.jsonl, and every sync clone — the exact paste the gate exists for. The contrast case proves the deciding branch: appending a single digit ('...flame7') makes the identical body fire. The design comment justifies the guard via 'a bare dictionary word', but a 25+ char hyphenated multi-word value following 'password is' is not that; the guard could require has_digit only for short/low-diversity values.
example_input: The family iCloud password is orbit-mango-velvet-cactus-flame
expected: generic-secret-assignment fires — a long passphrase directly assigned to 'password is' is a live secret
actual: [] — body commits cleanly; adding one digit to the same passphrase fires
verifier_notes: CONFIRMED. Repro reproduces verbatim at HEAD 874b0b0: the digit-less passphrase body returns [] and the identical body with one trailing digit fires generic-secret-assignment, proving has_digit (src/bettermemory/credentials.py:188-189) is the deciding branch. Severity medium, not high: the module explicitly accepts false negatives as a class (the gate is a best-effort tripwire, not a relied-upon scanner), and the failure is a missed backstop rather than corruption of a routinely-consumed signal. One important caveat on the claim: its proposed fix direction ("require has
suggested_fix:
In _looks_like_secret (src/bettermemory/credentials.py:187-189), keep has_digit as the default requirement but add ONE narrow letters-only escape hatch for the passphrase chain shape: replace `return has_alpha and has_digit` with:

    has_alpha = any(c.isalpha() for c in v)
    has_digit = any(c.isdigit() for c in v)
    if has_alpha and has_digit:
        return True
    # Letters-only diceware/"memorable" passphrase: 4+ word segments of 3+
    # alpha chars joined by - or _. Prose compounds after "password is"
    # ("case-sensitive", "auto-generated", "end-to-end-encrypted") have at
    # most 2-3 qualifying segments and stay silent.
    return has_alpha and bool(re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z]{3,}(?:[-_][A-Za-z]{3,}){3,}", v))

Verified against live code: this fires on 'orbit-mango-velvet-cactus-flame' and 'correct-horse-battery-staple' while staying silent on every measured prose collision ('case-sensitive', 'user-specific', 'auto-generated', 'alphanumeric', 'project-scoped', 'configurable', 'end-to-end-encrypted' — the last because 'to' is under 3 chars). Requiring 4+ segments deliberately leaves 3-word passphrases uncaught — that is the precision-over-recall posture the module documents. Add paired tests in tests/test_credentials.py: fires on 'the family iCloud password is orbit-mango-velvet-cactus-flame'; does NOT fire on 'the password is case-sensitive' and 'the password is auto-generated'. Also update the inline comment at lines 185-186 to name the passphrase exception so the next reader sees the trade-off explicitly.

title: Trailing '}' from YAML flow mappings / JS object literals trips the env-template guard — an unquoted password at the end of an inline mapping never fires
location: _looks_like_secret, line 167 (if v[0] in "$<{%" or v[-1] in ">}%")
description: The env-var/template-reference guard rejects any value whose LAST char is '>', '}', or '%'. The value regex [^\s\"']{8,} runs to the next whitespace, so when a secret is the final entry of a YAML flow mapping or unquoted JS/HCL-ish object paste — 'auth: {username: deploy, password: hunter2Abc9XyZ12Q}' (docker-compose/Ansible inline-dict style) — the closing brace is captured into the value, v[-1]=='}' matches the guard, and the value is misclassified as a {{template}} reference even though it neither starts with '{' nor contains a second brace. Contrast case: the same body with a space before '}' fires. The guard should require template shape on BOTH ends (or strip trailing brackets) instead of treating one trailing '}' as proof of a template.
example_input: auth: {username: deploy, password: hunter2Abc9XyZ12Q}
expected: generic-secret-assignment fires — a high-entropy mixed-class password directly assigned to 'password:'
actual: [] — commits cleanly; identical body with whitespace before the closing brace fires
verifier_notes: Confirmed false negative, exactly as claimed. In /Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/credentials.py, _GENERIC_KEYWORD_RE's value capture [^\s\"']{8,} (line 128) runs to the next whitespace, so in a YAML flow mapping where the password is the last entry ('auth: {username: deploy, password: hunter2Abc9XyZ12Q}') the closing brace is captured into the value; _looks_like_secret then hits line 167 'if v[0] in "$<{%" or v[-1] in ">}%"' and misclassifies the literal secret as a template reference. NOT a documented trade-off: the guard's comment (lines 165-166) targets actual template shapes ($VAR, ${VAR}, <your-key>, {{token}}, %SECRET%), and tests (tests/test_credentials.py lines 81-91) only cover values starting with $/<. The accident is unambiguous: 'auth: {password: hunter2Abc9XyZ12Q, username: deploy}' FIRES (trailing comma) while the same secret in last position is silent — position-dependent behavior inside one mapping. The module's precision-over-recall charter covers prose keyword mentions, not a pasted literal secret; this is the 'obvious paste' the docstring says the tripwire exists for, and the failure direction (secret silently persisted to a plaintext git-synced store) is the worst one for this module. Caveat on the claim's proposed fix: requiring template shape on BOTH ends would regress 'password = myapp-${VAULT_SECRET}' (embedded template ref, verified it currently and correctly returns []) — the trailing-char check is load-bearing for ope
suggested_fix:
In _looks_like_secret (src/bettermemory/credentials.py), treat a trailing closer as template evidence only when it is paired with an opener in the value; otherwise strip it as punctuation from the surrounding syntax before judging. Right after `v = value.strip().strip("\"'")` (line 162), add:

    # A trailing }/> is only template evidence when its opener appears in the
    # value ('myapp-${VAR}', '<your-key>'). A lone trailing closer is the
    # surrounding flow-mapping / object syntax — strip it before judging.
    if v and v[-1] == "}" and "{" not in v:
        v = v[:-1]
    elif v and v[-1] == ">" and "<" not in v:
        v = v[:-1]
    elif v and v[-1] == "%" and "%" not in v[:-1]:
        v = v[:-1]

and keep line 167 as-is. This preserves every documented guard case ($VAR, ${VAR}, <your-key>, {{token}}, %SECRET%, and embedded 'myapp-${VAULT_SECRET}' all retain their opener so the existing check still rejects them), runs before the length gate so a stripped 11-char value still bounces, and introduces no new false positives. Add regression tests: 'auth: {username: deploy, password: hunter2Abc9XyZ12Q}' fires generic-secret-assignment; 'password = myapp-${VAULT_SECRET}' stays [].

title: Code assignment operators ':=' (Go) and '=>' (Ruby hashrocket) defeat the single-char [:=] separator — pasted config code with a live password never fires
location: _GENERIC_KEYWORD_RE separator, line 127 (\s*(?:[:=]|\bis\b)\s*)
description: The separator accepts exactly one ':' or '=' (or the word 'is'). In 'password := "hunter2Abc9XyZ12Q"' the regex consumes ':' as the separator, then the next char is '=' which cannot start the >=8-char value run before the quote, so the whole match fails; same for Ruby's ':password => ...' where '=' is consumed and the leftover '>' kills the value. Memory bodies quoting a line of Go or legacy-Ruby config ('the test fixture hardcodes password := "..." in db_test.go') therefore commit with the literal secret intact, while the plain '=' spelling of the identical line is blocked. Distinct from the reported prose-phrasing gap ('is set to'): this is the code-operator family, fixable by allowing [:=]=? or :?= in the separator.
example_input: password := "hunter2Abc9XyZ12Q"
expected: generic-secret-assignment fires — same assignment as 'password = ...' which does fire
actual: [] for both ':=' and '=>' spellings; '[]' while 'password = "hunter2Abc9XyZ12Q"' fires
verifier_notes: REPRODUCED at HEAD 874b0b0. I attempted to refute and could not. Mechanism confirmed by dissecting the regex at /Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/credentials.py:127: in 'password := "hunter2Abc9XyZ12Q"' the separator alternation (?:[:=]|\bis\b) consumes ':' as the single separator char; the post-separator \s* cannot consume the leftover '='; the value class [^\s"']{8,} starting at '=' captures only 1 char before the quote/space kills it (needs 8+); and backtracking cannot reach the '=' as separator because the preceding \s* cannot skip over ':'. Same structure kills Ruby ':password => ...' (consumes '=', leftover '>'). Verified ALL four code-operator forms miss — Go ':=' quoted AND unquoted, Ruby '=>' quoted AND unquoted — while the byte-identical line with plain '=' or ':' fires. Refutation attempts that failed: (1) "documented trade-off" — the module docstring (lines 28-35) disclaims recall generally ("tripwire for the obvious paste, not a secret scanner"), but the generic rule's own header comment (line 113) states its target IS "the config-paste ... shape", and a pasted Go config line is squarely that target class; no comment or test pins ':='/'=>' as excluded (grep over tests/test_credentials.py: zero coverage of either operator), and the 'is' alternation shows intent to cover even prose connectives, making the code-operator miss an accident of the single-char alternation, not a choice. (2) "contrived input" — Go is a mainstream language whe
suggested_fix: In /Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/credentials.py line 127, widen only the separator alternation: r"\s*(?:[:=]|\bis\b)\s*" -> r"\s*(?:=>|[:=]=?|\bis\b)\s*" (ordered: '=>' first, then ':='/'=='/':'/'='). This is strictly a separator widening — the _looks_like_secret value gate (length 12-200, placeholder list, env-var/path/dotted-ref/SCREAMING_SNAKE rejections, charset-mix requirement) is untouched, so the documented precision-first design is preserved; the separator only decides which assignment-shaped lines get their value examined. Note '[:=]=?' also admits '==', which is correct behavior ('password == <high-entropy literal>' still embeds the secret) and the common benign form 'password == user.hashed_password' is already rejected by the dotted-ref check in _looks_like_secret. Verified against every negative fixture in tests/test_credentials.py (keyword-without-secret prose, placeholders, env-var refs, low-diversity values, config.SECRET_KEY-style dotted refs, paths): zero new fires; all seven positive forms (=, :, is, := quoted/unquoted, => quoted/unquoted) caught. Add two parametrized cases to test_detector_fires: ("generic-secret-assignment", 'password := "hunter2Abc9XyZ12Q"') and ("generic-secret-assignment", ":password => 'hunter2Abc9XyZ12Q'"), plus optionally a comment on line 127 noting the separator covers code assignment operators (:=, =>, ==) deliberately.

title: Numbered-list splitting glues the next item's index onto the previous fragment — bare section headers ('Action items:') are pushed over the MIN gate and flag 0.0 on fully grounded bodies
location: _SENTENCE_SPLIT_RE (line 66) / _split_sentences (lines 88-94), consumed by check_groundedness (lines 127-140)
description:
_SENTENCE_SPLIT_RE treats every 'digit-period-space' in a Markdown ordered list as a sentence boundary, so 'Action items:
1. Refresh the changelog
2. Ping the team' fragments as ['Action items:
1', 'Refresh the changelog
2', 'Ping the team']. Each list item's own index is split AWAY from it, and the NEXT item's index is glued onto the preceding fragment. The killer case is the header: a two-content-token header like 'Action items:' / 'Next steps:' / 'Key decisions:' would normally be skipped (< MIN_CONTENT_TOKENS=3), but the glued '1' promotes it to 3 tokens — and since transcripts essentially never contain the literal words 'action items', the header fragment scores 0.0 and flags as an ungrounded claim even when every actual list item is grounded verbatim in the transcript. The identical body written with dash bullets passes clean (dash bullets don't split — the already-reported merge bug — so the two list syntaxes fail in opposite directions). The glued index also corrupts item fragments themselves: it inflates the denominator of unpunctuated items ('Refresh the changelog
2' is 3 tokens instead of 2), shifting borderline paraphrases across the 0.30 threshold. Numbered checklists with a header are one of the most common realistic memory-body shapes (runbooks, decision lists, action items), and with groundedness_check=True this flag bounces the write.
example_input: body='Action items:\n1. Refresh the changelog\n2. Ping the team in Slack', transcript='User: after each release, refresh the changelog and ping the team in Slack.'
expected: No flags — every claim in the body is grounded verbatim in the transcript; the section header is layout furniture, not a claim (and at 2 content tokens it is below the gate's own evaluation floor).
actual: [UngroundedClaim(sentence='Action items:\n1', overlap_ratio=0.0)] — the header plus the stolen list index is flagged as a hallucinated claim; the same body with dash bullets returns [].
verifier_notes:
Reproduced exactly at HEAD 874b0b0: check_groundedness('Action items:
1. Refresh the changelog
2. Ping the team in Slack', transcript) returns [UngroundedClaim(sentence='Action items:
1', overlap_ratio=0.0)] while the dash-bullet equivalent returns []. Mechanism verified at token level: _SENTENCE_SPLIT_RE (src/bettermemory/groundedness.py:66, r"[.!?;]\s+|

+") splits at the 'digit. ' of each list marker, gluing the NEXT item's index onto the preceding fragment. The header fragment 'Action items:
1' has content tokens {1, action, items} = exactly 3, defeating the MIN_CONTENT_TOKENS=3 skip floor whose purpose is to exempt non-claims ('Action items:' alone is 2 tokens and would be skipped). The secondary denominator-inflation claim is also mechanically real ({2, changelog, refresh} = 3 tokens for a 2-content-token item). NOT a documented trade-off: the splitter comment (lines 61-65) accepts over-splitting only because "the resulting fragments still get checked independently and a real claim will still match the transcript" — false here on both counts (the manufactured fragment is layout furniture and cannot match any transcript). The CHANGELOG over-split-by-design entry concerns attribution.py, a different module. No numbered-list coverage in tests/test_groundedness.py. title: Comma-coordinated embellishment smuggling: a grounded head clause anchors a majority-fabricated sentence — the canonical 'extractor embellishes the fact' failure passes untouched
location: check_groundedness (lines 130-140) with _SENTENCE_SPLIT_RE (line 66) providing no sub-sentence boundary
description: The splitter has no boundary below [.!?;]/paragraph level, and the 0.30 threshold is a ratio over the whole sentence's token set. So when the extractor welds invented attributes onto a real preference with commas/conjunctions — the textbook HaluMem embellishment shape ('prefers X, lives in Y, and owns Z') — the grounded head clause supplies enough overlap to carry up to ~70% fabricated content tokens through the gate. In the repro, 'The user prefers tabs over spaces, lives in Tokyo with three cats.' passes at 4/9 = 0.444 although 5 of its 9 content tokens (lives, tokyo, three, cats + prefers) have zero transcript anchor; writing the identical fabricated material as its own sentence flags it at 0.0. The module's own docstring frames the gate as catching 'facts pulled from thin air', and per-sentence evaluation exists precisely so siblings can't dilute (see test_multiple_sentences_evaluated_independently) — but the most natural way a model embellishes is inside one sentence, where no boundary ever fires. Unlike the already-reported single-newline bullet-list merge, this needs no markdown structure at all: plain prose coordination defeats the gate.
example_input: body='The user prefers tabs over spaces, lives in Tokyo with three cats.', transcript='User: tabs over spaces, always — set indentation to tabs.'
expected: The fabricated 'lives in Tokyo with three cats' material should surface as ungrounded — it is exactly the thin-air content the gate exists to catch, and it IS flagged (0.0) when phrased as its own sentence.
actual: [] — the single comma-coordinated sentence passes at overlap_ratio 0.444; the hallucinated attributes commit silently inside an otherwise grounded memory.
verifier_notes: Repro confirmed verbatim at HEAD 874b0b0: one-sentence body 'The user prefers tabs over spaces, lives in Tokyo with three cats.' returns [] (overlap 4/9=0.444 >= 0.30) while the two-sentence variant flags 'Lives in Tokyo with three cats.' at 0.0. Token-level check: overlap={user,tabs,over,spaces}; {lives,tokyo,three,cats,prefers} have zero transcript anchor. This is NOT the docstring's accepted trade-off — that covers hallucinated sentences sharing 'generic vocabulary' (src/bettermemory/groundedness.py:30-33); here fabricated tokens share nothing and pass purely on the grounded head clause's dilution. Decisively, tests/test_groundedness.py:118-127 (test_sentence_split_on_semicolon_and_paragraph) documents the design property that fragments are evaluated independently 'so a body that uses semicolons can't smuggle an ungrounded clause inside a grounded sentence' — semicolon was added to _SENTENCE_SPLIT_RE (groundedness.py:66) precisely for anti-smuggling, yet comma coordination (the far more common clause joiner) bypasses it. Input shape is realistic: short comma-coordinated single sentences are the natural form of memory bodies, and welding invented attributes onto a real fact is the canonical extractor-embellishment failure. Severity tempered to medium because (a) the gate is opt-in (groundedness_check=False default) and advisory/overridable (handlers/write.py:357-386), and (b) the smuggling window is bounded — I verified a longer fabricated tail ('...and runs the full suite
suggested_fix: Do NOT add ',' to _SENTENCE_SPLIT_RE — that would shred legitimate enumerations ('prefers tabs, two-space YAML, and editorconfig') into fragments below MIN_CONTENT_TOKENS or spuriously flagged. Instead add a conservative second pass in check_groundedness (src/bettermemory/groundedness.py:130-140): for each sentence that PASSES the sentence-level threshold, split it on comma/coordination boundaries (e.g. re.split(r",\s+(?:and\s+|but\s+)?|\s+and\s+", sentence)), and flag a sub-clause only when it has >= min_content_tokens content tokens AND strictly zero overlap with the transcript (overlap_ratio == 0.0). Requiring zero anchor for sub-clauses keeps false positives near nil — a legitimate coordinated clause on the same topic almost always shares at least one content token with the transcript — while catching thin-air embellishment ('lives in Tokyo with three cats' -> 4 content tokens, 0 overlap -> flagged). title: Monorepo shared cwd: every path-citing write tagged with one sub-project is gated to add every sibling sub-project (identical roots, symmetric false flag)
location: detect_scope_mismatch pass-2 (lines 158-204, find at 176) + collect_project_roots (lines 222-246)
description: collect_project_roots maps each projects:<name> scope independently to its most-common origin.cwd. In a monorepo (one repo, several logical sub-projects each with its own projects:* scope), every session runs from the same checkout, so multiple scopes legitimately converge on the IDENTICAL root — no mis-attribution involved, every root is correct. Pass-2 then treats 'body contains root R of scope S, S not declared' as evidence, so a write correctly tagged projects:api that cites any absolute path under the monorepo also matches projects:webapp's (identical) root and is rejected with 'add projects:webapp' — and vice versa, symmetrically, on every single path-citing write for that repo. In that configuration, every write correctly tagged with one sub-project that cites any absolute path under the shared tree matches the sibling scope's identical root and is hard-Rejected by ScopeMismatchGate (src/bettermemory/handlers/write.py line 330) with kind='project_root', symmetrically in both directions. title: SSH-config Host-alias remotes (git@github-work:...) never match the canonical host — the standard multi-account GitHub setup splits one repo into two identities
location: _parse_remote / _SSH_REMOTE_RE host capture (line 519, group 1) consumed by repos_match (lines 133-158)
description: The single most common way the same GitHub/GitLab repo acquires two different remote spellings is an ~/.ssh/config Host alias: 'Host github-work / HostName github.com / IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_work' (or the 'github.com-work' dash-suffix convention every multi-account tutorial teaches). The clone URL becomes git@github-work:acme/billing-api.git. repos_match compares the literal host captured by _SSH_REMOTE_RE group 1 against the canonical github.com form, so the alias form never matches git@github.com:acme/billing-api.git or https://github.com/acme/billing-api — every memory written from the aliased clone is invisible (auto-scope filters it out) in a re-clone with the canonical URL, on a second machine with a synced store, or in commit-drift/audit surfaces that call repos_match. This is mechanically distinct from the already-reported insteadOf finding: insteadOf is git-level aliasing fixable by reading `git remote get-url`, whereas ssh-config aliases are invisible to every git command — only resolving the alias at capture time (e.g. `ssh -G <host>` hostname lookup) or treating alias-like hosts specially can close it. Also distinct from the reported ssh.github.com/altssh vendor-fallback-host finding, which is a fixed vendor equivalence; this is per-user arbitrary host strings.
example_input: repos_match('git@github-work:acme/billing-api.git', 'git@github.com:acme/billing-api.git') — memory written in a work-account clone, caller in a canonical-URL clone of the same repo
expected: True — both remotes are the same repository (the alias resolves to github.com in ~/.ssh/config)
actual: False — parsed triples ('github-work','acme','billing-api') vs ('github.com','acme','billing-api'); same for the 'github.com-work' dash-suffix convention
verifier_notes: CONFIRMED with one scope correction. Repro output matches the claim exactly: _parse_remote yields ('github-work','acme','billing-api') vs ('github.com','acme','billing-api') and both repos_match calls return False (including the 'github.com-work' dash-suffix form). Mechanism verified end-to-end: capture reads `git config --get remote.origin.url` (/Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/origin.py:297-298), which returns the literal alias spelling — ssh-config Host aliases are invisible to every git command, so no capture-side normalization rescues it. _SSH_REMOTE_RE (origin.py:519) captures the alias verbatim as host; repos_match (origin.py:133-158) compares (host,owner,name) literally, so the alias never equals the canonical form. NOT a documented trade-off: the parsing section comment (origin.py:512-517) only claims to handle "the two forms git config typically emits... plus a few less-common variants"; no comment, docstring, or test mentions ssh aliases. test_repos_match_different_hosts (tests/test_origin.py:147-151) pins github-vs-gitlab — genuinely different repos — not aliases. Nothing in the repo mentions insteadOf or ssh.github.com either, and the claim's mechanical distinction from those findings is sound (git-level rewriting vs ssh-level resolution vs fixed vendor equivalence). SCOPE CORRECTION (claim overstates the search surface): memory_search auto-scope goes through should_include_for_caller (origin.py:177-225, called at search.py:508-513)
suggested_fix: Resolve ssh-config aliases inside _parse_remote (origin.py:522) at match time, in one place, with no file-format change: when the URL matched _SSH_REMOTE_RE (scp-like) or has an ssh:// scheme, pass the captured host through a module-level lru_cache'd helper that runs `ssh -G <host>` (subprocess, ~1s timeout, mirroring the _git helper's swallow-failures discipline) and extracts the `hostname` line; use the resolved hostname as the comparison host, falling back to the literal host on any failure (ssh missing, timeout, no hostname line). This is conservative by construction: `ssh -G` is a pure local config parse (no network), and a host with no Host stanza resolves to itself, so equality only widens when the user's own ~/.ssh/config declares the alias — no risk of merging unrelated repos. Guard the host argument against option-injection (reject hosts starting with '-') before invoking ssh. The lru_cache keeps search over N memories at O(distinct hosts) subprocesses. Do NOT resolve only at capture time: legacy records and cross-machine stores already contain literal-alias spellings, so match-time resolution is required anyway and handles both sides symmetrically (capture-time canonicalization can be added later as an additive optimization). Add tests pinning: alias-with-stanza matches canonical (mock the ssh -G call), alias-without-stanza still fails closed, and ssh-unavailable falls back to current behavior.

title: HTTP mount-prefix remotes misparse the prefix as owner: Gerrit's authenticated '/a/' makes two HTTPS clones of the SAME project never match each other, and relative-URL GitLab/Apache '/git/' installs never match their SSH form
location: _parse_remote HTTPS branch, path.split('/', 1) at line 547 — first path segment unconditionally treated as owner
description: The urlparse branch assumes path[0] is the owner for every http(s) remote. On servers that mount git under a path prefix that assumption inverts the identity: (1) Gerrit prepends '/a/' to authenticated HTTP clone URLs — https://gerrit.corp.com/a/tools/build parses to owner='a', name='tools/build' while the anonymous clone of the SAME project (https://gerrit.corp.com/tools/build) parses to owner='tools', name='build'. Two HTTPS clones of one Gerrit project — differing only by whether credentials were configured at clone time — never match, and neither matches the SSH form. (2) GitLab installed under a relative URL root (https://intranet.corp.com/gitlab/team/app.git, a documented common install shape) and generic smart-HTTP-behind-Apache '/git/' mounts misparse the same way, so HTTPS and SSH remotes of one self-hosted repo never match. This generalizes beyond the already-reported Bitbucket-Server '/scm/' finding in two ways: it is not a single vendor's fixed prefix (any relative-URL install shape triggers it), and in the Gerrit case the mismatch is same-protocol HTTPS-vs-HTTPS, a failure shape the Bitbucket finding does not cover.
example_input: repos_match('https://gerrit.corp.com/a/tools/build', 'https://gerrit.corp.com/tools/build') — the authenticated and anonymous HTTP remotes of one Gerrit project; also repos_match('https://intranet.corp.com/gitlab/team/app.git', 'git@intranet.corp.com:team/app.git')
expected: True in both cases — same repository, the leading path segment is a server mount/route prefix, not an owner
actual: False in all cases — ('gerrit.corp.com','a','tools/build') vs ('gerrit.corp.com','tools','build'); ('intranet.corp.com','gitlab','team/app') vs ('intranet.corp.com','team','app')
verifier_notes: Reproduces exactly as claimed: _parse_remote (src/bettermemory/origin.py:537-550) unconditionally takes the first HTTP(S) path segment as owner, so 'https://gerrit.corp.com/a/tools/build' -> ('gerrit.corp.com','a','tools/build') while the anonymous URL of the same project -> ('gerrit.corp.com','tools','build'); repos_match returns False for all three claimed pairs. Not a documented trade-off: the comment block at origin.py:512-517 only lists accepted input shapes, and no test in tests/test_origin.py pins mount-prefix behavior; gerrit//scm//bitbucket appear nowhere in src, tests, or docs. The failure direction is the module's safe side — a false negative in the auto-scope UX filter (memory fails to surface; escape hatches: auto_scope=False, memory_show), not the cross-project leakage the module docstring names as the embarrassing failure mode. The claim is honest but only half-actionable, and it substantially overlaps the already-reported Bitbucket-Server '/scm/' finding it cites: (1) the Gerrit '/a/' half is a second fixed vendor prefix, fixable in the exact same prefix-strip table the Bitbucket fix would introduce — it is the same root cause and same fix shape, so it should be folded into that fix, not treated as a separate bug; the 'HTTPS-vs-HTTPS' novelty is a corollary, not a new code path. (2) The GitLab-relative-URL / Apache-'/git/' half is NOT fixable while preserving the documented conservative design: arbitrary prefixes are syntactically indistinguishable from owners
suggested_fix: Fold into the existing Bitbucket '/scm/' fix as ONE change: in _parse_remote's url-scheme branch (src/bettermemory/origin.py:543-550), after computing `path`, strip a known fixed vendor route prefix before the owner split — if the first segment is in a small frozen table {'scm' (Bitbucket Server), 'a' (Gerrit authenticated HTTP)} AND the remainder still contains a '/', drop it: `first, _, rest = path.partition('/'); if first in _VENDOR_ROUTE_PREFIXES and '/' in rest: path = rest`. The remainder-contains-'/' guard keeps github.com/a/repo (real single-char owner) parsing as owner='a'. Residual cost: a single-char group 'a' WITH a subgroup on a GitLab host would now mismatch its SSH form — a far rarer false negative than the Gerrit case fixed, and it stays in the conservative (no-leakage) direction. Do NOT add generic prefix-stripping or path-suffix matching for the GitLab-relative-root/'/git/' case — that merges distinct subgroup projects (cross-project leakage, the documented worst failure mode); instead document that limitation in the comment block at origin.py:512-517 and add tests pinning both the new prefix handling and the deliberate non-handling of arbitrary mounts.

title: Event-log rotation mid-window archives the turn's own search event — the retrieval shield reads only the active log and a searched-then-continued turn emits a false search_miss
location: _count_recent_retrievals (lines 550-584) fed from iter_events (active log only) at handlers/audit_turn.py:123 and hook.py:231; rotation semantics in events.py _rotate_if_needed (lines 293-332, rename of the WHOLE active log)
description: Both audit producers build the shield's event list via `list(iter_events(store.root))`, which by contract never reads rotated archives. Rotation (`_rotate_if_needed`) fires on the record() call that finds the active log >= max_bytes (default 10 MB) and atomically renames the ENTIRE active log into a .gz archive — including events written seconds earlier. So on the turn where the log crosses the threshold: the model's memory_search event is appended (pre-append size check still under the limit), any later event in the same turn (an auto-commit `use`, a `write`, a `verify`) triggers rotation and sweeps the search event into the archive, and the end-of-turn audit then sees recent_retrieval_count=0 and flags 'miss' on a turn that demonstrably searched. The comment at handlers/audit_turn.py:117-121 ('rotation thresholds are far larger than that window in normal use, so a search event from this session within the window is still in .events.jsonl') conflates window length with rotation timing — rotation archives by file, not by age, so an in-window event is lost whenever the crossing happens mid-turn. The hook.py module docstring even acknowledges the active-log bound for scope_disable replay ('the shielded miss RE-FIRES') but the retrieval shield has the same hole. With per-turn turn_audited telemetry the log grows continuously, so every store recurringly crosses the boundary. Counterfactual with iter_all_events shields correctly.
example_input: Long-lived store with .events.jsonl at ~9,999,940 bytes (months of telemetry). Turn: model runs memory_search ('myapp deploy', returns the relevant memory), then an auto-commit `use` event lands; user message 'restart the docker compose stack' matches a stored memory 3/3. Stop-hook audit runs within the 60s window.
expected: verdict 'ok' (recent_retrieval_count=1 — the model searched seconds ago in this session)
actual: verdict 'miss', recent_retrieval_count=0: the `use` record rotated the whole log (search event included) into .events-<ts>.jsonl.gz, which iter_events never reads. Reading archives (iter_all_events) yields 'ok' / count=1.
verifier_notes: CONFIRMED, despite the adversarial stance — the claim survives every refutation angle. (1) Repro reproduces exactly: production (active log) -> verdict 'miss', recent_retrieval_count=0; counterfactual (iter_all_events) -> 'ok', count=1, with the search event visible only in the .gz archive and the active log containing only the 'use' event. (2) The mechanism is in the real production paths, not just the harness: events.py record() runs _rotate_if_needed() BEFORE the append (src/bettermemory/events.py:234-235), so the append that crosses max_bytes never rotates itself — the NEXT record() os.replace()s the ENTIRE active log into the archive (events.py:371), sweeping the seconds-old search event. In the in-process audit, handlers/audit_turn.py:114 calls _advance_turn, which itself records the auto-commit 'use' event (handlers/_shared.py:299-306) immediately before line 123 reads list(iter_events(...)) — the audit handler's own bookkeeping can be the rotation trigger that blinds its shield. The stop-hook path (hook.py:231) has the same hole via any post-search record in the turn. (3) Not a documented trade-off: the comment at handlers/audit_turn.py:116-121 asserts a factually wrong invariant ('a search event from this session within the window is still in .events.jsonl') — it reasons from window age vs rotation threshold, but rotation archives by file, not age. hook.py's 'Residual divergence' docstring (lines 54-57) documents the active-log bound only for scope_disable replay and
suggested_fix: Add a window-aware reader in src/bettermemory/events.py — e.g. iter_recent_events(root, *, cutoff: datetime) — that yields active-log events and, ONLY when the active log does not cover the window (empty/missing, or its earliest parseable ts is newer than cutoff), additionally reads the single newest archive (reuse the existing _archive_sort_key ordering) and yields its events too. Cost stays bounded: the archive decompression happens only during the brief post-rotation window (until the active log accumulates an event older than the 60s lookback), preserving the per-turn audit's O(active-log) common path and the module's conservative design. Use it at the two audit producers: handlers/audit_turn.py:123 and hook.py:231 (cutoff = now - max(lookback, _ATTRIBUTION_LOOKBACK_SECONDS) for the hook, since the same list feeds attribution). Rewrite the now-disproven comment at handlers/audit_turn.py:116-121 to state the actual rule (rotation archives by file, not age; the newest archive is consulted only when the active log doesn't span the window). Add a regression test mirroring the repro: fill the log to just under max_bytes, record search then use, assert probe_for_miss with the production reader returns 'ok' with recent_retrieval_count=1. Leave the documented scope_disable replay residual in hook.py as-is (it needs full-history semantics, is explicitly accepted in the docstring, and biases the opposite direction); optionally note that feeding the widened list to _disabled_scopes_from_events also narrows that residual.

title: Probe cannot thread recency_boost_half_life_days or endorsement_boost — it ranks with hardwired defaults while production search uses the configured values, so the rank-1-only verdict diverges from the model's actual ranker
location: probe_for_miss run_search call, lines 428-437 (no half_life_days / applied_by_id arguments; run_search defaults half_life_days=30.0); contrast handlers/search.py:274-292 which threads config.behavior.recency_boost_half_life_days and endorsement counts
description: The module's stated design rule is 'probe matches the model's configured search mode... probing with a different scorer than the model would have used measures the wrong thing' — and the handler dutifully threads `mode`. But mode is not the whole ranker: production memory_search also threads `half_life_days=deps.config.behavior.recency_boost_half_life_days` (config.py:290, a documented [behavior] knob) and, when `endorsement_boost=true` (config.py:307), per-memory applied counts. probe_for_miss has no parameters for either, so the probe always ranks with half_life=30.0 and no endorsement nudge. Because the v1 threshold reads ONLY the rank-1 hit, any near-tie (within the 10% recency/endorsement band — exactly the fresh-partial-match vs old-exact-match shape the dogfood data shows is common) is broken differently by the probe than by the ranker the model actually uses. Verified false-negative: with a user-configured half_life of 2 days, the model's own search puts the 3/3 'high' memory at rank 1 (a genuine v1 miss when no search fired), but the probe's default-30 ranking puts a fresher term-frequency-heavy 'medium' partial match at rank 1 and reports 'ok'. The mirror false-positive (probe flags a miss whose top-1 under the model's config would have been 'medium') follows by symmetry whenever the configured value pushes the fused order the other way.
example_input: Config: [behavior] recency_boost_half_life_days = 2, search_mode = 'keyword'. Store: memory A (300 days old) 'flaky postgres testcontainers teardown: disable ryuk to stop the hangs.'; memory B (5 days old) 'postgres tuning: bumped postgres shared_buffers and postgres wal level; postgres replica teardown is manual.'. User message: 'flaky postgres testcontainers teardown'; no retrieval this turn.
expected: Probe ranks with the model's configured ranker: top-1 = A, relevance 'high' -> verdict 'miss' (the model's own search would have surfaced a high-relevance top hit it never looked for)
actual: Probe ranks with the hardwired 30-day half-life: top-1 = B, relevance 'medium' -> verdict 'ok'; the silent miss is never flagged. (probe_for_miss exposes no way for either producer to pass the configured value.)
verifier_notes: Reproduced exactly as claimed at HEAD 874b0b0: with [behavior]-style half_life=2.0 the model's own ranker puts memory A (exact 4/4 coverage, 'high') at rank 1, while probe_for_miss — which has no half_life parameter and lets run_search default to 30.0 — puts the fresher partial match B ('medium') at rank 1 and returns verdict 'ok', swallowing the silent miss. Code facts all verify: (1) public search() accepts half_life_days=30.0 and applied_by_id=None (src/bettermemory/search.py:758-772); (2) production memory_search threads both from config (src/bettermemory/handlers/search.py:266-283, half_life_days=deps.config.behavior.recency_boost_half_life_days at line 283, applied_by_id via _explicit_applied_counts when endorsement_boost is on); (3) probe_for_miss (src/bettermemory/audit.py:311-323) exposes only mode, and its run_search call (audit.py:428-437) passes neither knob; (4) both producers — handlers/audit_turn.py:131-141 and hook.py:253-263 — thread mode=config.behavior.search_mode but structurally cannot thread the other ranker parameters. This is NOT a documented trade-off: the module docstring's own design rule (audit.py:25-31) says probing with a different scorer than the model would have used measures the wrong thing, and the only documented deliberate exclusions are expand_top/path_drift, explicitly justified as consumption-side signals (audit.py:353-355) — half_life and endorsement are scoring-side and change which hit the rank-1-only v1 rule reads. Both false-negativ
suggested_fix: Minimal threading change preserving the module's conservative design and side-effect-free probe. (1) In src/bettermemory/audit.py, add two keyword params to probe_for_miss — half_life_days: float = 30.0 and applied_by_id: dict[str, int] | None = None — and forward both in the run_search call at lines 428-437; extend the existing 'probe matches the model's configured search mode' docstring note to cover all configured ranker parameters (mode, half-life, endorsement counts), keeping the expand_top/path_drift exclusion as-is. Defaults keep every existing offline/test caller byte-identical. (2) In src/bettermemory/handlers/audit_turn.py (~line 132), thread half_life_days=deps.config.behavior.recency_boost_half_life_days, and when deps.config.behavior.endorsement_boost is true reuse the existing _explicit_applied_counts helper from handlers/search.py to pass applied_by_id, mirroring memory_search exactly. (3) In src/bettermemory/hook.py (~line 253), thread half_life_days=cfg.behavior.recency_boost_half_life_days; for the hook's endorsement counts either tally explicit-applied events in the same event-log pass it already makes for the lookback shield, or, if deferred, add an explicit docstring note that the hook probe omits the endorsement nudge — making the residual divergence documented instead of silent. Add a regression test pinning the repro shape: custom half-life, old-exact vs fresh-partial near-tie, assert probe verdict matches the verdict computed from the config-threaded ranker.

title: Demotion treats contradiction-flagged memories as dead weight, and the retag's `updated` bump silently clears health's unresolved-contradiction signal
location: find_demotion_candidates (lines 427-449) + the apply-path retag in consolidate() (lines 734-735); interacts with health.MemoryStats.has_unresolved_contradiction (health.py:127-156)
description: Demotion eligibility checks only created/retrieved/applied. A memory carrying an unresolved record_use(contradicted) event — the bucket health.py parks for mandatory resolution via memory_update or memory_verify — satisfies all three (retrieved > 0, applied == 0, age > 30d) because 'contradicted' is a `use` outcome that never increments `applied`. So the unattended stop-hook auto-consolidate demotes a known-wrong fact to category=ambient ('response-shaping context that informs every reply'). Worse, the retag goes through Store.update, which unconditionally stamps `updated`; has_unresolved_contradiction clears as soon as `updated` surpasses last_contradicted_at, because it treats any update as a resolution ('the body has been refreshed in response to the contradiction'). The metadata-only retag therefore launders the contradiction flag: the contradicted bucket empties with no body refresh and no verification, the wrong content stays active as ambient, and the curation signal that existed to force resolution is extinguished by the very pass that documents itself as 'nothing requiring judgment'.
example_input: Memory 'Staging API base URL is https://staging.api.acme.dev' (fact, created 60d ago); events: one search returning it 10d ago, one record_use(contradicted, note='staging moved to staging2.api.acme.dev') 5d ago. Nightly auto-consolidate runs before the user resolves it.
expected: A memory with an unresolved contradiction is excluded from dead-weight demotion (it is awaiting explicit resolution, not lacking value), and in any case a category-only retag must not read as a contradiction resolution in memory_health.
actual: find_demotion_candidates returns it as a demotion candidate (current_category='fact' -> 'ambient'); after the retag (updated bumped by Store.update), compute_health's contradicted bucket goes from [id] to [] — flag gone with zero resolution.
verifier_notes:
Attempted to refute; could not. The claimed repro runs verbatim and every link in the chain checks out against real code paths.

REPRO (verbatim, PYTHONPATH=src venv/bin/python):
demotion candidates: [{'memory_id': '01ARZ3NDEKTSV4RRFFQ69G5FA1', 'summary': 'Staging API base URL is https://staging.api.acme.dev (behind the VPN).', 'age_days': 60, 'retrieved_count': 1, 'current_category': 'fact', 'proposed_category': 'ambient'}]
contradicted BEFORE retag: ['01ARZ3NDEKTSV4RRFFQ69G5FA1']
contradicted AFTER retag: []

The repro's one simulated step (model_copy bumping `updated`) is faithful to production: /Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/consolidate.py:734-735 does `memory.model_copy(update={"category": Category.AMBIENT})` then `store.update(new_memory)`, and Store.update at /Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/store.py:492-493 unconditionally stamps `updated = utcnow()` ("Overwrite an existing memory in place; bump `updated`"). The event shapes in the repro (`kind="use"`, `ids`, `outcome`; `kind="search"`, `returned`) match what handlers/record_use.py:164 and the search recorder actually write.

WHY IT IS A REAL BUG, NOT A DOCUMENTED TRADE-OFF:
1. The overlap is structural, not contrived. A contradicted memory is by construction "retrieved but not applied" for that interaction (the contradicted outcome overrides the auto-applied commit). So any fact-category memory older than window_days (default 30) carrying an unresolved c
suggested_fix:
Minimal fix preserving the pass's documented conservative design — exclude unresolved-contradiction memories from demotion eligibility in find_demotion_candidates (/Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/consolidate.py:398-449). The function already iterates all events; additionally track per-id last-contradicted timestamps:

In the event loop (after line 422), add:
    if event.get("outcome") == "contradicted":
        ts = parse_event_ts(event.get("ts"))   # already imported-adjacent helper used elsewhere in the module
        if ts is not None:
            prev = last_contradicted.get(mid_key)
            ... track max ts per id in `last_contradicted: dict[str, datetime]`

Then in the candidate loop (after the applied check at line 436-437), skip when the contradiction is unresolved, mirroring health.MemoryStats.has_unresolved_contradiction without importing health:
    lc = last_contradicted.get(memory.id)
    if lc is not None:
        resolved_at = memory.updated
        if memory.last_verified_at is not None and memory.last_verified_at > resolved_at:
            resolved_at = memory.last_verified_at
        if lc > resolved_at:
            continue  # parked in health's contradicted bucket awaiting explicit resolution — not dead weight

This makes "skip unresolved contradictions" hold for BOTH the dry-run report and the apply path (auto and manual), keeps the contradicted health bucket intact until a genuine memory_update/memory_verify resolution, and matches the run_auto_consolidate docstring's "no contradiction resolution" promise. Update the find_demotion_candidates docstring to note the exclusion, and add a regression test in tests/test_consolidate.py: memory with a contradicted use event newer than updated/last_verified_at is not a demotion candidate; one with a contradiction older than a later verify/update still is.

(A second-layer hardening — making metadata-only retags not bump `updated` via a Store.update flag — would also stop the flag-laundering but weakens the optimistic-concurrency CAS semantics documented at store.py:450-458; the eligibility exclusion above is sufficient and far less invasive.)

title: propose_new's provenance stamp is system-manufactured boilerplate that defeats Jaccard dedup: the second distinct fact from the same turn is rejected as a 'near-duplicate'
location: _apply_llm_proposal ProposeNewProposal branch — provenance stamping at lines 1549-1555, find_similar gate at lines 1591-1607; pairs scored by _find_dedup_jaccard (lines 297-329)
description: Every `consolidate --llm --from-transcript` propose_new body gets '\n\n_(consolidate --llm --from-transcript: <verbatim turn excerpt>)_' appended. When one user turn carries two distinct durable facts (the normal case — e.g. dotfiles location AND shell setup in one sentence), both proposals cite the same literal turn, so both bodies share an identical excerpt whose tokens dominate the Jaccard sets: each distilled fact's content tokens are largely a subset of the shared quote. Measured: two clearly distinct facts score 0.882 with the stamp vs no dedup candidate at all without it. Consequences: (a) within one apply loop, the first fact commits and every subsequent fact from the same turn is rejected by the gate's find_similar high check (Jaccard high threshold 0.75) with 'propose_new body high-overlaps existing memory' — silent capture loss behind a misleading reason; (b) if both ever coexist (e.g. written under a semantic-model gate, which embeddings-based similarity would not confuse), the next manual `consolidate --apply` (Jaccard 0.75) tombstones one distinct fact as a near-duplicate. The dedup heuristic is being fed boilerplate the system itself stamped on.
example_input: Transcript turn: 'My dotfiles live in ~/dotfiles and I manage them with GNU stow; my shell is zsh with the starship prompt.' LLM proposes fact A 'User manages dotfiles in ~/dotfiles with GNU stow.' and fact B 'User's shell is zsh with the starship prompt.', both stamped with the same excerpt.
expected: Two distinct facts distilled from one turn both commit; similarity is judged on the claims, not on the audit-provenance stamp shared by construction.
actual: Jaccard similarity 0.882 (control without the stamp: no candidate generated at all). find_similar labels the pair 'high' at 0.882, so _apply_llm_proposal raises 'propose_new body high-overlaps existing memory' for the second fact; find_dedup_candidates flags the pair above the 0.75 manual --apply threshold.
verifier_notes: Adversarial stance could not refute this; it is a genuine false-signal bug, and verification surfaced a second failure direction the claim missed. (1) Repro ran verbatim and matched the claim exactly: with the provenance stamp the two distinct facts score Jaccard 0.882 ('high'), firing both find_similar's 0.75 high gate and find_dedup_candidates' 0.75 manual --apply threshold; the control without the stamp produces no candidate at all. (2) End-to-end through consolidate_llm (FakeProvider, apply=True, accept=True, from_transcript) on HEAD 874b0b0: the first ProposeNewProposal commits, the second distinct fact fails with 'propose_new body high-overlaps existing memory <id of the first>' — only one of two facts lands. The apply loop (consolidate.py:1355-1384) is sequential and the ProposeNew branch calls store.load_all() fresh (line 1593), so the first stamped write is always visible to the second proposal's gate. (3) Not a documented trade-off: the adjacent transient-marker gate (consolidate.py:1571-1589) was explicitly scoped to proposal.body for this exact root cause — provenance is a verbatim transcript quote that contaminates gate scans — with a regression test (tests/test_consolidate_llm.py:590, test_propose_new_writes_durable_body_despite_transient_provenance) whose docstring states the principle. The similarity gate at 1591-1617 passes body_with_provenance instead, with no comment accepting the contamination; this is the same bug class fixed once and missed at the next g
suggested_fix: Two minimal changes, both preserving the conservative stamp-in-body audit design. (1) In /Users/mattias/Documents/projects/bettermemory/src/bettermemory/consolidate.py, ProposeNewProposal branch: pass proposal.body (not body_with_provenance) to find_similar (line ~1596) and find_similar_tombstones (line ~1612), exactly mirroring the transient-gate scoping at lines 1573-1582 and extending its documented rationale (gates judge the LLM-authored claim, not the audit citation); keep the max_content_bytes check on body_with_provenance since that is what persists. Verified this both clears the false positive (gate on proposal.body vs the stamped sibling: no hit) and is necessary for true-dup detection anyway, since comparing against stamped bodies is what dilutes real duplicates. (2) For already-stamped stored bodies (both sides of the comparison in later runs and in the manual consolidate --apply dedup pass): add a small _strip_provenance(body) helper using a regex anchored to the system's own stamp format, e.g. re.sub(r"\n\n_\(consolidate --llm --from-transcript: .*?\)_\s*$", "", body, flags=re.DOTALL), and apply it to memory bodies before tokenizing/embedding in _find_dedup_jaccard (line 301) and _find_dedup_semantic (line 343), and to stored-memory bodies inside find_similar's comparison path used by the consolidate gates. Only the machine-generated stamp is excluded; user-authored text is never stripped. (3) Add regression tests mirroring test_propose_new_writes_durable_body_despite_transient_provenance: (a) two ProposeNewProposals with identical source_excerpt and distinct bodies both commit; (b) a true near-duplicate of an already-stamped memory is still rejected by the gate; (c) find_dedup_candidates does not pair two stamped distinct facts above 0.75.

title: find_cold_scopes has no ambient exclusion: all-ambient scopes are flagged 'consider archiving' for lacking the applied signal that is structurally absent for ambient by design
location: find_cold_scopes (lines 454-509) — no Category.AMBIENT check anywhere in the pass
description: The project's own design says ambient memories are 'excluded from the dead-weight rule because their value is implicit' (models.py Category docstring), and health.py excludes ambient from both dead_weight and cold_memories with the rationale that 'the use signal is structurally absent and a count of zero there is not an indictment' (health.py:1292-1299). One real-world mitigation tempers severity: the auto-record_use flow mints use-tokens for ALL hits including ambient (handlers/_shared.py _attach_use_tokens has no category filter) and auto-commits them as applied ~2 turns later, and consolidate() feeds find_cold_scopes the FULL event history (consolidate.py:620-630), so a single lifetime auto-applied suppresses the suggestion forever. The claim's "weekly searches, zero a
suggested_fix:
In find_cold_scopes (src/bettermemory/consolidate.py, inside the `for scope, scope_memories in by_scope.items():` loop, before the max_created check), skip scopes composed entirely of ambient memories, mirroring the structural exemption the demotion pass applies at line 429 and health.py's dead_weight/cold exclusion:

    if all(m.category == Category.AMBIENT for m in scope_memories):
        # All-ambient scope: ambient value is implicit (uncited by
        # design), so a lifetime of zero applied events is not

title: Cold-scope pass: a single applied event ever grants permanent immunity — finished-but-once-useful project scopes (the most common archivable shape) are never suggested for archiving
location: find_cold_scopes, applied_ids lifetime set (lines 479-491): `if any(m.id in applied_ids for m in scope_memories): continue` with applied_ids built from the full unwindowed event history
description: The pass exists to surface scopes worth archiving, but the applied-event exemption has no time bound: applied_ids is accumulated over the entire event history (iter_all_events, active log + all rotated archives), so any scope where even one memory fired record_use(applied) once — years ago — is exempt forever, no matter how long ago its newest memory was created or how dead it has been since. The most realistic archivable scope is exactly this shape: a completed project that WAS useful while alive (so it has a handful of ancient applied events) and has been untouched since the project ended. Such scopes can never trigger the suggestion; the only scopes the pass can flag are ones that never produced value at all. The docstring acknowledges the lifetime semantics ('no applied events ... in any window'), but that calibration structurally blinds the heuristic to its primary target population — the signal it exists to raise is silently missed on the canonical input. (Contrast: the 180-day staleness gate is windowed on created; the value gate is not windowed on anything.)
example_input: Scope 'projects:thesis-pipeline' with 3 memories created 900/800/700 days ago and two applied events 650 and 600 days ago; zero events of any kind since.
expected: A scope whose newest memory is ~2 years old and whose last applied event is ~20 months old is a prime 'consider archiving' candidate.
actual: find_cold_scopes returns no suggestion for the scope (the 600-day-old applied event exempts it permanently); the identical scope with the two applied events removed IS flagged.
verifier_notes: CONFIRMED despite adversarial stance. Verified on HEAD 6fb74d2 (one commit past claimed 874b0b0; git diff shows src/bettermemory/consolidate.py unchanged between them). (1) Repro reproduces exactly: scope with applied events 650/600 days old -> no suggestion; identical scope with no applied events -> flagged.
